items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Billings, MT
items.meta: Billings is Montana's refining and pipeline hub, but that's different from being a drilling hotspot. A retired E&P engineer explains what actually drives mineral value here.

sections.html:
Billings runs Montana's oil business at the refining and pipeline level, which is a different thing entirely from having active drilling under the city itself.

As the state's largest city and the seat of Yellowstone County, Billings has been the commercial center of Montana's oil and gas industry for a century, home to refineries and the offices of companies that operate wells hundreds of miles away in the Bakken or Powder River Basin. If you own mineral rights on a tract in or near Billings, though, that industrial presence doesn't automatically mean your specific acreage has been drilled or leased.

sections.title: Industry Headquarters Versus Local Production
sections.html: It's a distinction we explain often. A company might have an office tower in Billings and a producing well in Richland County, three hundred miles away, with no connection between the two beyond the corporate address. Evaluating your Billings-area mineral interest means looking at what's actually recorded and permitted on your specific tract, not the broader industry presence in the city.

sections.title: Ownership History in the Yellowstone Valley
sections.html: Land in and around Billings was largely settled and irrigated under early twentieth-century homestead and reclamation projects, with mineral rights frequently severed from the surface at some point as the city grew and agricultural land changed hands. Confirming your exact recorded interest against the current chain of title at the courthouse is the real first step, particularly for interests that have passed through several generations.

sections.title: What we'd Actually Check
sections.html: We pull the recorded deed, check for any historical or current lease on the specific parcel, and look at whether there's realistic nearby activity, which for most in-city and near-city tracts, there isn't. We'll give you an honest range based on what the title and permit records actually show, not the city's reputation as an oil town.

faqs.q: Does Billings have active oil and gas drilling within the city?
faqs.a: Generally no. Billings functions as a refining, pipeline, and corporate hub for companies operating wells elsewhere in the state, not as an active drilling area itself.

faqs.q: Where do you check the title on mineral rights in Yellowstone County?
faqs.a: The Yellowstone County Clerk and Recorder in Billings holds the recorded deeds, leases, and division orders for the entire county.

faqs.q: Why would your mineral rights near Billings be worth less than a Bakken county tract?
faqs.a: Value follows actual production and permitting activity on your specific tract, not a city's industry reputation. Most Yellowstone County acreage near Billings has limited or no drilling history, which is a fair, honest starting point for any offer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Yellowstone County, MT
items.meta: Yellowstone County minerals aren't a drilling headline, they're refining infrastructure and scattered legacy fields. A retired engineer explains what that means for a sale.

sections.html:
Billings refines other counties' oil more than it produces its own, and mixing those two things up is the first mistake sellers make here.

Yellowstone County is Montana's most populated county, and Billings sitting in the middle of it is the biggest city in the state by a wide margin. That size gives people the wrong impression sometimes. Billings has long been a refining town, home to plants that process crude piped in from the Powder River Basin, the Bakken, and Canada, and it's easy to look at those stacks and assume the ground underneath the county is loaded with production to match.

It isn't, not really. What Yellowstone County has is a handful of small, older conventional fields scattered around its edges, a lot of split ownership left over from railroad and homestead-era land grants, and a downstream industry that has nothing to do with whether your particular section ever produced a barrel.

sections.title: Billings Is a Refining Hub, Not a Drilling Hub
sections.html:
The crude that keeps Billings' refineries running mostly arrives by pipeline from somewhere else, Wyoming's Powder River Basin, the Bakken up north, and Canadian heavy crude. That infrastructure creates jobs and tax base in Yellowstone County, but it says nothing about mineral production directly beneath any given parcel here.

We've talked to landowners who assumed a nearby refinery meant their minerals were automatically valuable. What actually matters is whether there's a producing or permitted well on or near your specific tract, and in most of Yellowstone County there isn't one.

sections.title: The Scattered Legacy Fields That Do Exist
sections.html:
There are small, older conventional pools around the county's edges, near Molt and Broadview toward Golden Valley County, and a handful of modest fields closer to Billings itself. These were mostly found decades ago, produce shallow formations, and decline slowly rather than dramatically. None of them are the kind of thing that shows up in industry headlines.

If you own minerals in one of these areas, the honest read is a small, steady royalty rather than a windfall. That's still worth something to a buyer looking for predictable cash flow, just not at the kind of price a fresh Bakken horizontal would command.

sections.title: Railroad Grants and Ranch-Era Split Estate
sections.html:
Part of what makes title work here different from a homestead county further east is the Northern Pacific Railroad's old land grant checkerboard, which ran through this stretch of Montana in alternating sections as part of the railroad's 19th-century federal grant. Minerals under those sections have their own severance history separate from the standard homestead patents, and it shows up in the chain of title as a different kind of reservation language.

Add in the straightforward ranch and dryland homestead severances that happened everywhere else in the county, and you end up with a patchwork where two neighboring quarter-sections can have completely different ownership stories underground.

sections.title: Records, Heirship, and the County Clerk's Office
sections.html:
The Yellowstone County Clerk and Recorder's office in Billings handles a lot more volume than a small rural county, which cuts both ways: records tend to be better organized, but there's also more competition for the office's time. Because it's the largest county in the state, mineral interests here have often been divided among more heirs, many of whom scattered out of Montana entirely over the generations.

If you're the one holding a fractional interest that traces back through a great-grandparent's ranch, expect the title work to involve tracking down cousins you've never met before a sale or lease can close. That's normal for a county this size and this old, not a red flag specific to your parcel.

faqs.q: Does living near Billings' refineries mean there's oil under your land?
faqs.a: No. Billings refines crude piped in from Wyoming, the Bakken, and Canada. Whether your specific parcel in Yellowstone County has ever produced depends on nearby well history, not the refinery skyline.

faqs.q: What if your minerals trace back to a railroad land grant?
faqs.a: Northern Pacific's old checkerboard grant created its own mineral severance pattern across parts of Yellowstone County, separate from homestead severances. Your title chain will show which kind of reservation applies to your section.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Yellowstone County minerals have ever produced anything?
faqs.a: Check well records through the Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation for activity near your legal description, or ask a landman to run it for you. Most of the county has no production history at all.

faqs.q: Should you expect the same kind of offer as someone in the Bakken counties?
faqs.a: No. Yellowstone County's legacy fields are older, smaller, and slower-declining than a Bakken horizontal. A fair offer here reflects that steadier but modest profile, not Williston Basin numbers.

faqs.q: Where do you start if you just found out you own a fractional interest here?
faqs.a: Pull the deed and patent chain from the Yellowstone County Clerk and Recorder's office, confirm whether the interest has been through probate, and check for producing or permitted wells nearby before talking value with anyone.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Sidney, MT
items.meta: Sidney, MT is the real center of Montana's Bakken, near the original Elm Coulee discovery. We buy mineral interests here based on actual decline curves.

sections.html:
Sidney is the county seat and, honestly, the center of gravity for Montana's whole Bakken story.

Elm Coulee Field, the discovery that proved the Bakken could be drilled horizontally at scale, sits right in Richland County around Sidney, years before anyone talked about North Dakota's boom. That gives Sidney-area mineral interests a real, two-decade production history behind them, not speculative edge-of-play potential. What it also means is that a lot of those original wells are mature now, well into decline, sometimes infilled with newer wells on the same unit. We evaluate a Sidney interest against that full picture, not against what a single royalty statement from a decade ago suggested it was worth.

The town itself grew fast through the 2010s boom years, and it's settled into a steadier rhythm since, which mirrors what's happened underground. We want callers from Sidney to have that same grounded expectation before we talk about their specific interest.

sections.title: Mature wells, real decline
sections.html: If your check has shrunk over the years, that's the expected shape of a horizontal Bakken well's life, not a red flag. We look at where the specific well or unit sits on its decline curve before we put a number in front of you, because that curve drives value more than anything else at this stage of the field's life.

sections.title: Twenty years of leasing history to untangle
sections.html: Sidney-area interests have often been leased, re-leased, pooled, and amended multiple times since the early 2000s. We pull the full chain from the Richland County Clerk and Recorder and cross-check it against Montana Board of Oil and Gas records before we make an offer, because a shortcut here is how a buyer ends up quoting the wrong number.

faqs.q: Is Sidney really tied to the original Bakken discovery?
faqs.a: Yes — Elm Coulee Field near Sidney was the first large-scale horizontal Bakken play, discovered around 2000, ahead of the North Dakota boom.

faqs.q: Why is your royalty check lower than it used to be?
faqs.a: Most likely natural well decline. Horizontal Bakken wells drop steeply after their first few years, and that's normal, not a sign of mismanagement.

faqs.q: How do you handle a lease history that's been amended several times?
faqs.a: We pull the complete recorded chain and cross-check it against state production records ourselves before making an offer.

faqs.q: Did the 2010s boom change what's under the ground, or just the town?
faqs.a: Mostly the town and the pace of infill drilling. The underlying decline curve on the original Elm Coulee wells followed its own timeline regardless of the surface activity.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Richland County, MT
items.meta: Richland County is where the Bakken actually started — Elm Coulee Field, discovered 2000. We buy mineral interests here based on real, now-mature decline curves.

sections.html:
If you want to talk about the Montana side of the Bakken honestly, you start in Richland County, because this is where the whole play actually began.

Most people think the Bakken boom started in North Dakota. It didn't. Elm Coulee Field, discovered in Richland County around 2000, was the first place anyone drilled the Bakken horizontally at real scale, years before Williston became a household name. That gives this county a genuinely different mineral history than the rest of Bakken MT — this isn't edge-of-play speculation, it's core acreage with two decades of real production behind it.

What that means for a mineral owner today is a maturity question more than an activity question. A lot of the original Elm Coulee wells were drilled between roughly 2000 and 2006, which puts them fifteen to twenty-five years into their production life. Horizontal Bakken wells decline steeply in the first few years and then settle into a long, low tail. If your family's interest has been receiving smaller checks than it did a decade ago, that's the well aging, not necessarily a sign anything's wrong.

sections.title: Two generations of Bakken wells on the same acreage
sections.html: Because Richland County was drilled early, a lot of the original spacing has since been infilled with newer wells using modern completion techniques, sometimes on the very same units as the original Elm Coulee wells. That means a single mineral interest here can be tied to a mix of a mature original well and a newer, better-completed one, which complicates the decline picture in a way that actually matters for valuation. We look at the whole unit's production history, not only one well's number.

sections.title: Sidney, Savage, and the rest of the county
sections.html: Sidney sits at the center of the county's oil economy and saw real Bakken-boom growth through the 2010s. Savage and the smaller communities to the south have their own pockets of Elm Coulee-era development, sometimes quieter than what's around Sidney but no less real. We check the specific section, not only the town name, before we say what an interest is worth.

sections.title: Title complexity from twenty-plus years of activity
sections.html: Twenty-plus years of leasing, re-leasing, unitization, and pooling in Richland County means the deed chain on an active mineral interest here can be genuinely complicated — original leases, amendments, unit agreements, sometimes multiple operators over the life of a single well. We do that work ourselves, pulling everything from the Richland County Clerk and Recorder in Sidney and cross-checking it against Montana Board of Oil and Gas production records before we make an offer.

sections.title: What decline actually means for your check
sections.html: A well that produced a strong royalty check in 2012 is very likely producing a fraction of that now, purely from natural decline, regardless of commodity price. We explain that math plainly rather than let a family assume a lower recent check means something's being mishandled. Understanding where a specific well sits on its decline curve is the single biggest factor in what we can offer for an interest tied to it.

sections.title: How the 2010s boom reshaped the county without changing the subsurface story
sections.html:
Sidney and the surrounding towns grew fast through the boom years, with workforce housing and new infrastructure built to keep pace with drilling activity. That surface-level growth ran on its own timeline, separate from the underlying decline curve of the original Elm Coulee wells, which followed the geology and the completion techniques of their era regardless of how busy the towns above them got.

We mention that distinction because families sometimes tie their expectations to how active the county felt during the boom rather than to what a specific well or unit is actually producing today. Those are two different measures, and only one of them determines value.

sections.title: Heirship across a well-documented but complicated county
sections.html: Because Richland County has such a long, active leasing history, we regularly find mineral interests split among several heirs from an original family severance, sometimes further complicated by multiple pooling or unitization agreements layered on top over the decades. We buy directly from an individual heir's confirmed fractional share and do the work of untangling the rest of the chain ourselves.

faqs.q: Is Richland County really part of the original Bakken discovery?
faqs.a: Yes. Elm Coulee Field here was drilled horizontally around 2000, years before the North Dakota boom, making this genuinely core Bakken acreage rather than an edge play.

faqs.q: Why is your royalty check smaller than it was ten years ago?
faqs.a: Almost certainly natural well decline. Horizontal Bakken wells drop steeply in early years and settle into a long low tail — that's the well aging, not a sign of a problem.

faqs.q: Could your interest be tied to more than one well?
faqs.a: Yes, common here given decades of infill drilling on original Elm Coulee-era units. We look at the whole unit's production, not a single well's number.

faqs.q: How complicated is the title work in Richland County?
faqs.a: More than most counties, given the leasing, unitization, and pooling history that's built up over twenty-plus years. We do that work directly through recorded county and state records.

faqs.q: Is Sidney the only active area, or does it extend into smaller towns?
faqs.a: Activity extends south into Savage and other smaller communities, though it varies section by section. We check your specific parcel before quoting.

faqs.q: Does the county still feel as busy as it did during the 2010s boom?
faqs.a: Not in the same way — that was a surface-activity peak tied to drilling pace, and it's settled since. It doesn't directly reflect where a given well sits on its decline curve today.

faqs.q: Your family's interest is split among several heirs — can you still buy your share?
faqs.a: Yes. We buy directly from an individual heir's confirmed fractional share without requiring the rest of the family to participate.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Roosevelt County, MT
items.meta: Roosevelt County sits mostly within the Fort Peck Reservation, where trust-land fractionation shapes mineral title more than the Bakken does. We buy interests here.

sections.html:
Most of Roosevelt County sits inside the Fort Peck Indian Reservation, and that fact shapes mineral title here more than the Bakken boom ever did.

We want to be direct about what makes Roosevelt County different from its Bakken MT neighbors. A large share of the land here is held in trust for individual Indian allottees or for the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes, administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs rather than through a straightforward fee-simple county record. Original allotments from the early 1900s have passed down through generations without consolidation, and it's common for a single quarter-section of trust land to carry dozens, sometimes hundreds, of fractional heir interests today. That's a different reality than a fee mineral interest in Richland or Sheridan County, and we don't pretend the process is the same.

The county also has real, older oil history — the Poplar Field near the town of the same name was discovered back in 1952, well before anyone talked about the Bakken by name, and it's been in slow decline for decades. Bakken-era horizontal activity has touched the fee acreage in the county too, mostly on non-trust land where leasing follows the standard state process.

sections.title: Trust land versus fee land — two different processes
sections.html: If your family's interest is trust land, any transaction runs through BIA approval, and we're upfront that this takes longer and follows a different set of rules than a private mineral sale. If it's fee land, meaning it was patented out of trust status at some point and is privately owned, the process looks like anywhere else in Montana, through the county clerk and recorder. We confirm which situation applies before we go any further, because the two aren't interchangeable.

sections.title: Allotment fractionation, plainly explained
sections.html: The original 1900s-era allotments in this county were often 160 or 320 acres to a single individual. A century of inheritance without consolidation means that same allotment can now be split among a large number of descendants, each holding a tiny fractional interest, sometimes so small the BIA has to combine multiple heirs' shares just to issue a single lease payment. If you're one of those heirs and you've never received anything meaningful from your share, that's consistent with what fractionation across this county typically looks like, not a sign your interest doesn't exist.

sections.title: The Poplar Field and its long decline
sections.html: Poplar Field is one of the older producing fields in this part of Montana, discovered in 1952 and still producing at low, mature rates. It sits on a mix of trust and fee land, which means the same trust-versus-fee distinction applies even to interests tied to this established field. We check both the production history and the land status before discussing value.

sections.title: What we check before making an offer here
sections.html: First, whether your interest is trust or fee land. Second, if fee, we pull the recorded chain from the Roosevelt County Clerk and Recorder in Wolf Point. If trust, we work through what BIA approval will require and we're honest about the added time. Either way, we look at nearby production, whether Poplar Field-related or newer Bakken-era activity, before we say what an interest is worth.

sections.title: Multiple heirs on a single allotment
sections.html:
It's common for us to find five, ten, sometimes dozens of co-owners holding fractional shares of the same original allotment, most of them scattered well outside Montana and unaware of who else in the family holds a piece. We buy individual fractional interests directly from a single heir — you don't need the rest of the family to agree to sell for us to make you an offer on your own share.

This matters because a lot of families assume a sale requires unanimous consent among every cousin who holds a fraction. It doesn't, for the interest that's actually yours.

sections.title: Working with a slower federal process without losing patience
sections.html: BIA-administered transactions move at the government's pace, not mine, and we won't pretend otherwise. What we can control is doing our own homework completely before submitting anything, so the process isn't slowed further by incomplete paperwork on our end. We'd rather front-load that effort than leave a family waiting longer than necessary.

faqs.q: Is your Roosevelt County mineral interest trust land or fee land?
faqs.a: It depends on your family's specific parcel and whether it was ever patented out of trust status. We confirm this first, since it determines the entire process.

faqs.q: What does BIA approval mean for selling a trust-land interest?
faqs.a: It means the transaction has to go through Bureau of Indian Affairs review rather than a simple county-recorded deed transfer. It takes longer, and we explain that timeline upfront.

faqs.q: Your family's allotment interest is tiny — is it even worth pursuing?
faqs.a: Often yes, even a small fractional heir share. We buy these regularly and don't skip the work just because the percentage is small.

faqs.q: Is the Poplar Field still producing?
faqs.a: Yes, at low, mature rates after decades of decline since its 1952 discovery. We check the current production tied to your interest before quoting.

faqs.q: Does Bakken activity reach into Roosevelt County?
faqs.a: On some fee acreage, yes, though the county's story is shaped more by trust-land fractionation and the older Poplar Field than by the newer Bakken boom.

faqs.q: Do all the heirs on your family's allotment need to agree before you can sell your share?
faqs.a: No. We buy individual fractional interests directly from a single heir. You don't need the rest of the family on board to sell what's yours.

faqs.q: Why does a BIA-administered sale take so much longer?
faqs.a: It runs through federal review rather than a simple county-recorded deed transfer. We do our own paperwork thoroughly upfront so we're not adding delay on top of the federal timeline.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Sheridan County, MT
items.meta: Sheridan County sits on the thin western edge of the Bakken, not the core. We buy mineral interests here based on the honest decline curve, not ND-style hype.

sections.html:
We'll say this straight to any Sheridan County family up front: you're on the edge of the Bakken, not in the middle of it, and that difference matters to what your minerals are worth.

We ran wells across the Williston Basin long enough to know exactly where the pay thins out, and Sheridan County sits right at that pinch. The Bakken and underlying Three Forks are real here — there's been genuine horizontal drilling activity along the county's eastern and southern edges since the boom years — but net pay thins noticeably compared to the core counties across the North Dakota line, and well economics reflect it. Fewer wells per section, longer payouts, and operators who've been more selective about where they'll drill.

Underneath that newer Bakken story is an older one most people outside the industry never hear about. Sheridan County had conventional Madison-formation production going back to the original Williston Basin discoveries in the 1950s, long before anyone talked about the Bakken by name. A lot of older family mineral interests in this county trace to leases and severances from that earlier era, layered now under newer Bakken-era leasing on the same legal descriptions.

sections.title: Why we don't quote Sheridan County like Richland or Williams County, ND
sections.html: It would be easy to let a family assume their Sheridan County interest is worth what a cousin's Bakken interest in North Dakota core acreage sold for. It isn't, and we won't let that comparison stand uncorrected. Well density here is lower, and a meaningful share of the county's leased acreage was drilled selectively rather than developed on the same tight spacing you'd see closer to Williston. That's not a knock on the county — it's just the honest edge-of-play reality, and it's exactly why we look at your specific unit's actual production rather than county-wide headlines.

sections.title: The Madison-era layer underneath
sections.html: If your family's mineral interest was originally leased in the 1950s or 60s for conventional Madison production, that lease may have expired decades ago, or it may have been re-leased when Bakken interest picked up in the 2000s and 2010s. We check both layers of history — the old conventional record and the modern unconventional one — because they can produce very different pictures of what's actually being paid on the same legal description today.

sections.title: Where the activity actually concentrates
sections.html: Within Sheridan County, drilling has leaned toward the areas nearer the Bakken's stronger extension rather than spread evenly county-wide. Parcels near Plentywood, Medicine Lake, and the eastern county line have seen more real activity than ground further west and north toward the Saskatchewan border, where interests tend to be quieter and more speculative. We check where your specific section falls in that picture before we say anything about value.

sections.title: Split-estate and BLM considerations
sections.html: Some ground in this county carries federally reserved mineral interests from earlier homestead patents, and where that applies, the BLM's own leasing and permitting process runs alongside — sometimes ahead of, sometimes behind — state permitting on adjacent private minerals. If your family's interest sits on split-estate ground, we confirm whether it's state, private fee, or federally administered before we say what we can offer, because those are three different transactions with three different processes.

sections.title: Heirship across generations of quiet ownership
sections.html: A fair number of Sheridan County interests we run into trace back to Scandinavian and Central European homestead families who settled this corner of Montana in the early 1900s, with mineral rights passed down through three or four generations since. We regularly find several heirs holding a single fractional interest, most unaware of the others, and we buy directly from any one of them without requiring the whole family to act together.

sections.title: What we tell every Sheridan County caller upfront
sections.html: We'd rather lose a phone call to an honest answer than win one with an inflated promise we can't back up once we've pulled the title and production record. That's the standard we hold ourselves to on every parcel in this county, whether it's a strong Bakken-era interest near Westby or a quiet homestead severance near Redstone.

faqs.q: Is Sheridan County part of the real Bakken boom?
faqs.a: Part of it, on the thinner western edge. Net pay and well density here don't match the core counties in North Dakota, and we price interests against that honest reality rather than boom-era headlines.

faqs.q: Your family's lease is decades old — is it Bakken or something older?
faqs.a: Possibly conventional Madison-formation production from the 1950s or 60s, later re-leased during the Bakken years. We check both layers of history on your parcel.

faqs.q: Does location within the county matter that much?
faqs.a: Yes. Activity concentrates more toward the eastern county line and Plentywood, while ground further west and north tends to be quieter. We check your specific section rather than quoting a county average.

faqs.q: How does split-estate or BLM land change a sale?
faqs.a: It adds a step to confirm whether your interest is state, private fee, or federally administered minerals, since each follows a different leasing and transfer process.

faqs.q: Why should you trust an edge-of-play valuation over a bigger number?
faqs.a: Because a number that doesn't match the actual production and lease record falls apart during closing. We'd rather quote you accurately the first time.

faqs.q: Your family's interest is split among several heirs who've never met — can you still buy your share?
faqs.a: Yes. We buy individual fractional interests directly and don't require every heir to participate for us to purchase your specific portion.

faqs.q: Are you honest even when the news isn't great for your parcel?
faqs.a: Yes. We'd rather tell you your interest is quiet ground with modest value than inflate a number that won't hold up once we've done the title and production work.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Baker, MT
items.meta: Baker, MT is the site of one of Montana's first oil discoveries and the Fallon County seat. A retired engineer explains what that century-old history means for your minerals.

sections.html:
Baker had a producing oil well before most of the Bakken counties existed as an idea, and that 1919 discovery is still the reference point for anything we evaluate here.

As the Fallon County seat, Baker is where the courthouse records for the surrounding Cedar Creek Anticline sit, and that anticline is genuinely historic ground. The discovery well drilled near town in 1919 was one of Montana's first commercial oil strikes, targeting shallower conventional zones rather than the shale that made headlines eighty years later. A lot of mineral title in and around Baker has been through multiple rounds of leasing since then, which makes the paper trail worth real attention.

sections.title: A Century of Layered Leasing
sections.html: When a field has been producing since 1919, chances are your family's interest has been leased, released, and re-leased more than once, sometimes to different operators targeting different zones at different times. We've pulled Fallon County title files that show three or four distinct leasing episodes across a single tract. Sorting out which lease is currently active and what your net revenue interest actually is under that lease takes real courthouse work, not a guess based on an old document in a family file.

sections.title: Cedar Creek Anticline Versus the Newer Bakken Edge
sections.html: Baker-area production has historically come from the Red River and Charles formations along the anticline, conventional targets that decline slowly and predictably compared to a shale well. Newer Bakken and Three Forks interest does extend toward this part of Fallon County from the more active core farther north, but it's thinner here, and we check current permitting specifically before assuming your tract has both kinds of potential.

sections.title: What we'd Look At for a Baker-Area Tract
sections.html: We start with your current division order if you're already receiving royalty, compare it against the recorded chain of title, and check the well's production decline over the last few years. For undeveloped acreage nearby, we look at whether it's closer to the older Cedar Creek trend or the newer Bakken-edge activity, since that shapes which buyers are actually interested and at what range.

faqs.q: Why is Baker, MT significant to Montana's oil history?
faqs.a: The Cedar Creek Anticline discovery well near Baker in 1919 was one of the first commercial oil strikes in the state, decades before the Bakken shale play developed. Production along this trend has continued, in slow decline, for over a century.

faqs.q: Is your Baker-area mineral interest Cedar Creek Anticline or Bakken?
faqs.a: It could be either, or both. Pull your lease and division order history at the Fallon County Clerk and Recorder in Baker to see which formation your current production, if any, comes from.

faqs.q: Why does an old well from decades ago still pay royalties?
faqs.a: Conventional fields like those along the Cedar Creek Anticline decline slowly and can produce economically for many decades. A modest, steady royalty check from an old well is a real, valuable asset even without new drilling.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Fallon County, MT
items.meta: Fallon County minerals sit on the Cedar Creek Anticline, one of Montana's oldest oil trends. A former engineer explains what that older-field history means.

sections.html:
Fallon County was producing oil before most people had heard the word Bakken, and that older-field history changes how we'd evaluate a mineral offer here compared to the newer shale counties.

Baker is the county seat, and it's also where Montana's oil business more or less started. The Cedar Creek Anticline runs the length of Fallon County, and the discovery well near Baker in 1919 was one of the first commercial oil strikes in the state, decades before anyone was talking about the Bakken formation as a target. That history matters practically, not only as trivia, because it means a lot of the county's mineral title has been through multiple rounds of leasing, drilling, and re-leasing over a century, and the paper trail can be more layered than a tract that's only seen one round of Bakken-era development.

We split our thinking on Fallon County minerals into two buckets. There's Cedar Creek Anticline production, which taps shallower conventional zones like the Red River and Charles formations along that structural high, and there's the newer Bakken and Three Forks interest that came in with the 2000s shale boom and extends into the county from the more active core in Richland and McKenzie Counties to the east. Knowing which bucket your tract falls in changes what a reasonable offer looks like.

sections.title: The Cedar Creek Anticline: Old Production, Steady Decline
sections.html:
This anticline has been producing for a century in places, which means wells here are typically far along their decline curve, with royalty checks that are smaller and steadier than a newly drilled Bakken well but also more predictable in the near term. If your family's interest has been generating a modest, consistent check for decades off an old Cedar Creek well, that's a different asset than a fresh Bakken unit, and we value it differently, usually weighting the remaining reserve life and current decline rate over any hope of a big new completion nearby.

A lot of the mineral ownership tied to this trend traces back to early homestead-era severances, sometimes with multiple small fractional owners after generations of inheritance. Confirming your actual net revenue interest against the recorded division order is the first real step, because the percentage on an old lease document doesn't always match what's currently being paid.

sections.title: Where the Bakken Edge Reaches Into Fallon County
sections.html:
The core of Montana's Bakken activity sits to the north in Richland and Roosevelt Counties, but Fallon County catches some of that play's western and southern extension, generally thinner pay and more marginal economics than the Elm Coulee area. If your tract has newer Bakken or Three Forks leasing activity on it, alongside or instead of Cedar Creek Anticline production, that's worth flagging specifically, since it changes both the value conversation and which buyers are interested.

We're candid with Fallon County owners that this is flank territory for the shale play, not core. Operators here are more selective about where they drill, and a lot of leased acreage in the county sits held-by-production off older wells rather than seeing fresh horizontal completions. That's not a knock on the county, it's just an honest read on where it sits relative to the play's best rock.

sections.title: Building an Honest Offer
sections.html:
For Cedar Creek Anticline interests, we weigh decline curve, remaining reserve life, and how consistent the operator has been on payment. For Bakken-edge interests, we weigh recent permitting activity, whether nearby units have actually been drilled or just leased, and how your acreage compares to the better-performing parts of the play farther north. Either way, we start with your title and your actual division order, not a guess.

Anyone offering you a flat number for Fallon County minerals without asking which trend your tract sits under, Cedar Creek or Bakken edge, hasn't done the homework. We'd rather walk through both possibilities with you honestly than give a round figure that doesn't hold up once someone actually checks the well records.

faqs.q: What is the Cedar Creek Anticline and why does it matter for your minerals?
faqs.a: It's a long structural trend running through Fallon County that's produced conventional oil since 1919, one of the oldest fields in Montana. If your interest sits along this trend, you're likely looking at a mature, slow-decline asset rather than newly drilled Bakken production, which changes how it should be valued.

faqs.q: Is Fallon County part of the core Bakken play?
faqs.a: No, it's on the flank. The core is farther north in Richland and Roosevelt Counties. Fallon County catches the play's thinner southern and western edge, so Bakken economics here tend to be more marginal than the core area.

faqs.q: How do you find out which trend your Fallon County tract sits under?
faqs.a: Start with a title search at the Fallon County Clerk and Recorder in Baker to pull your lease and division order history. That record will show whether your interest has been developed under older Cedar Creek Anticline wells, newer Bakken units, or both.

faqs.q: Why would an old, low-producing well still be worth something?
faqs.a: A mature well with a predictable, if modest, decline curve still generates real royalty income, and that income stream has value even without new drilling. We weigh remaining reserve life and payment consistency rather than assuming an old well means a worthless interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Powder River County, MT
items.meta: Powder River County is the actual Powder River Basin, but the thinner Montana edge of it. We buy CBM and fee mineral interests here based on real production.

sections.html:
This is the county the whole basin is named for, and it's also honestly the thinner northern edge of it.

Powder River County sits at the top of the Powder River Basin, the same coal-seam gas trend that made Campbell County, Wyoming one of the most heavily developed CBM areas in the country. The Montana side never matched that density. Wyodak and Anderson coal-seam gas leasing reached into this county during the 2000s CBM boom, and some units are still producing, but well spacing here has generally been wider and development more selective than across the state line. If your family's interest is in Powder River County, we want you to understand that comparison honestly before we ever discuss a number.

Almost all the land in this county is fee land — there's no reservation trust status to navigate here, unlike Big Horn or Rosebud County to the north. That simplifies the process considerably, even though the underlying activity picture is more modest.

sections.title: Why the Montana side of the Powder River Basin is thinner
sections.html: Coal seam thickness, depth, and water handling economics all shift as you move north from the Wyoming core into Montana, and operators followed that economics — concentrating drilling where the coal was thickest and cheapest to produce. Powder River County saw real leasing and real wells, but nothing close to the saturation seen in Campbell County. We evaluate an interest here against that honest baseline.

sections.title: What a lapsed CBM lease looks like here
sections.html: A lot of 2000s-era CBM leasing in this county had short terms, and when gas prices fell in the following decade, plenty of acreage reverted to the mineral owner unleased. If your family hasn't seen a payment in years, that's consistent with a lapsed lease rather than mismanagement, and we check the recorded status before saying anything about value.

sections.title: Ranch-family ownership and Broadus records
sections.html: Powder River County is ranch country, and a lot of mineral interests here trace to homestead-era severances kept separate when a ranch was sold or passed down through a family. We pull the recorded chain from the Powder River County Clerk and Recorder in Broadus before we make any offer, confirming exactly who holds what share.

sections.title: How we price interests on the thin edge of a named basin
sections.html: We look at whether the parcel sits inside a still-active CBM spacing unit, on lapsed leasehold, or on ground that was never leased at all. Each of those is a genuinely different asset, and we won't collapse them into one number just because they all sit inside the county the basin is named for.

sections.title: Water disposal and why it shaped this county's development
sections.html: Coalbed methane production requires pulling large volumes of water out of the coal seam to release the gas, and handling that water was expensive here, more so than in parts of the Wyoming core with better disposal options nearby. That economic reality, as much as the geology itself, is why Powder River County never saw the well density its southern neighbor did. It's worth understanding if you're trying to make sense of why some units near your family's parcel were drilled and others, on paper similar ground, never were.

sections.title: Broadus courthouse realities for older ranch families
sections.html: A lot of the families we work with in this county have deep roots going back three or four generations on the same ranch, with mineral rights that were carved off in a sale decades ago and largely forgotten since. The Broadus courthouse holds that whole history, and we go through it methodically rather than asking a family to reconstruct decades of paperwork themselves.

faqs.q: Is Powder River County as active as the Wyoming side of the basin?
faqs.a: No, and we say that plainly. Development here has always been thinner and more selective than the Campbell County, Wyoming core.

faqs.q: Is your mineral interest trust land or fee land?
faqs.a: Almost certainly fee land — there's no reservation trust status in this county, which simplifies the sale process.

faqs.q: Your CBM lease hasn't paid anything in years — is it still active?
faqs.a: Possibly not. A lot of 2000s-era leases here had short terms and lapsed when gas prices fell. We check the recorded status before quoting.

faqs.q: How do you verify ownership in this county?
faqs.a: Through the recorded deed chain at the Powder River County Clerk and Recorder in Broadus, the same as any ranch-country parcel in eastern Montana.

faqs.q: Is a never-leased interest here worth anything?
faqs.a: Often yes, priced as long-term potential rather than current income. We explain that distinction clearly before making an offer.

faqs.q: Why did some units in the county get drilled and neighboring ones didn't?
faqs.a: Largely water disposal economics. CBM production requires handling significant water volumes, and that cost was higher here than in parts of the Wyoming core, which made operators more selective.

faqs.q: Your family's mineral rights were carved off a ranch sale decades ago — can you still trace that?
faqs.a: Yes. We work through the Broadus courthouse records methodically to reconstruct that history rather than asking you to piece it together yourself.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Rosebud County, MT
items.meta: Rosebud County splits between Northern Cheyenne trust land and the Colstrip coal belt. We buy mineral interests here, coal, CBM, and oil and gas, honestly.

sections.html:
Rosebud County is really two mineral stories stitched together — Northern Cheyenne trust land on the west side, and the Colstrip coal belt on the east.

We treat Rosebud County as two distinct territories because that's what the record actually shows. The western part of the county sits within the Northern Cheyenne Reservation, where mineral interests can be trust land administered through the Bureau of Indian Affairs or fee land held privately, sometimes both within the same extended family. The eastern part of the county is home to the Rosebud Mine, one of the larger surface coal operations in the state, feeding the Colstrip power plant, plus scattered coalbed methane leasing tied to the broader Powder River Basin trend that runs south into Powder River County and beyond.

A family calling us from Lame Deer is usually navigating a different question than a family calling from Rosebud or Forsyth, and we don't apply the same process to both without checking first.

sections.title: Trust land on the Northern Cheyenne side
sections.html: If your interest is trust land, a sale runs through BIA approval, and we're honest that this adds time to the process compared to a standard county-recorded deed. We confirm land status early through BIA records rather than assuming based on the town name alone.

sections.title: The Rosebud Mine and Colstrip coal economy
sections.html: The Rosebud Mine has operated for decades supplying coal to the Colstrip Steam Electric Station, and mineral ownership tied to that ground often carries coal-specific deed language separate from any oil and gas rights. We read the actual severance language before assuming your family's interest covers both.

sections.title: Coalbed methane on the county's Powder River Basin edge
sections.html: The eastern and southern parts of Rosebud County touch the northern extension of the Powder River Basin CBM trend, the same coal-seam gas play that runs more densely through Wyoming to the south. Leasing here has been real but less consistent than in the trend's core, and we check current status before quoting.

sections.title: What we confirm before making an offer
sections.html: First, whether the interest is trust or fee land, and if trust, what tribal or individual allotment structure applies. Second, whether the mineral deed covers coal, oil and gas, CBM, or some combination. Third, current lease and production status on the specific parcel. We do all of that through Rosebud County records in Forsyth and BIA records as needed before we put a number in front of a family.

sections.title: Why we treat this county parcel by parcel, not as one story
sections.html:
We've had callers from Rosebud County assume their situation matches whatever their neighbor described, only to find their own parcel sits on the opposite side of the trust-fee line, or carries a completely different mineral severance. Given how much this county genuinely varies within its own borders, we don't shortcut that verification for anyone, regardless of how confident the initial description sounds.

That care takes a little longer up front, but it's the only way we can stand behind a number once we've quoted it.

sections.title: Forsyth as the county's record center
sections.html: For any fee-land transaction, Forsyth is where the paper trail lives, and it's where we start every search regardless of which town in the county the family is calling from. For trust land, we work in parallel through the relevant BIA agency office covering Northern Cheyenne allotments.

sections.title: Heirship on both sides of the county
sections.html: Whether trust or fee, mineral interests in Rosebud County have often passed through multiple generations without formal consolidation. We regularly buy from a single heir holding a fractional share, on either side of the reservation boundary, without requiring the rest of an extended family to participate in the sale.

faqs.q: Is your interest near Lame Deer trust land?
faqs.a: Possibly, if it's within the Northern Cheyenne Reservation. We check BIA records to confirm before discussing the sale process.

faqs.q: Does your family own coal rights, oil and gas rights, or both near Colstrip?
faqs.a: It depends on the original severance deed. We read the actual language to confirm rather than assuming a full-mineral package.

faqs.q: Is there coalbed methane activity in Rosebud County?
faqs.a: In parts, tied to the northern edge of the Powder River Basin trend, though less dense than the core play in Wyoming. We check your specific parcel.

faqs.q: Where do you check fee-land ownership in this county?
faqs.a: The Rosebud County Clerk and Recorder in Forsyth, for any parcel outside trust status.

faqs.q: Why does the process differ so much within one county?
faqs.a: Because Rosebud County genuinely spans two different land-tenure systems. We confirm which one applies to your specific interest before anything else.

faqs.q: Your neighbor described a very different situation than mine — is that normal here?
faqs.a: Yes. This county genuinely varies parcel to parcel between trust and fee status and between coal, CBM, and oil and gas rights. We verify your specific situation independently.

faqs.q: Where do you start a Rosebud County title search?
faqs.a: Forsyth for fee land, through the county clerk and recorder. For trust land, we work in parallel through the relevant BIA agency office.

faqs.q: Do all the heirs need to agree before you can sell your share?
faqs.a: No, whether your interest is trust or fee land. We buy directly from a single heir's confirmed share without requiring the rest of the family to participate.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Big Horn County, MT
items.meta: Mineral owner in Big Horn County, MT near the Crow Reservation? A former engineer explains trust-land title, BIA approval steps, and how offers get built here.

sections.html:
Big Horn County is the one place in this state where we tell owners to expect their sale to run through two agencies instead of one, because most of the county sits inside the Crow Reservation.

We spent enough years running drilling and workover programs on the Powder River Basin's western edge to know Big Horn County by its paperwork as much as its geology. Hardin is the county seat, the Bighorn River cuts the county roughly in half, and the Crow Indian Reservation covers most of the ground from Crow Agency and Lodge Grass down through Fort Smith and Wyola. That reservation boundary is not a footnote here. It is the single biggest factor in how a mineral sale actually closes.

Where we'd usually tell a Montana seller the surface is BLM and the minerals were severed off an old homestead patent, Big Horn County flips that script for a large share of owners. A lot of mineral interest in this county traces back to individual Indian allotments made under the Crow Allotment Act, which means the Bureau of Indian Affairs, not only the county clerk, has a hand in who can buy, sell, or lease. If your family's interest came down through an allotment, that changes the timeline and the paperwork, and we'd rather tell you that up front than have you find out three weeks into a deal.

sections.title: Trust Land, Fee Land, and Why It Matters to Your Sale
sections.html:
Big Horn County's mineral ownership splits into two broad buckets. Fee minerals are owned outright and transfer the way minerals do anywhere else in Montana, by deed, through the clerk and recorder in Hardin. Trust minerals are held in trust for an individual Crow tribal member or the tribe itself, with the BIA holding legal title and the allottee or their heirs holding the beneficial interest. You cannot sell a trust mineral interest with a simple warranty deed. It requires BIA approval of the transaction, often a fair-market-value determination on their end, and a longer clock than a fee sale.

We've seen owners assume their interest is trust because a grandparent was enrolled Crow, when in fact the interest was patented in fee decades ago and sells like any other Montana mineral estate. We've also seen the reverse, where a family thought they owned fee minerals free and clear and the BIA layer surfaced only when a landman pulled the chain of title. The honest first step is a title check at the courthouse and, if there's any Crow allotment history in the family, a call to the BIA Crow Agency office to confirm whether your specific interest is still trust or was fee-patented out.

sections.title: What's Producing Around Hardin, Crow Agency, and Fort Smith
sections.html:
Big Horn County sits on the far western edge of the Powder River Basin, which is coalbed methane country more than it's a deep shale play. The CBM boom of the late 1990s and 2000s put wells into the Fort Union coals across parts of the county, particularly toward the Rosebud County line, and some of that production is still on the books, aged and shallow-decline. There's older conventional production too, tied to structures along the basin's flank, but nothing here compares to the drilling intensity of the Bakken counties on the state's eastern edge.

Fort Smith and the Bighorn Canyon National Recreation Area sit at the county's south end near Yellowtail Dam, mostly federal and tribal recreation land with limited oil and gas activity. Most of the interest we get asked to evaluate here is small, fractional, and inherited, split among heirs over two or three generations from an original allotment or homestead patent, producing a modest royalty check off an old well rather than sitting under active drilling.

sections.title: Building a Fair Offer on Big Horn County Minerals
sections.html:
We build an offer here off the same fundamentals we'd use anywhere: what's the well's current decline curve, is there any active permitting nearby, what does your net revenue interest actually calculate to once we've confirmed the recorded chain of title, and whether the tract sits near the CBM-productive belt or out in the quieter reservation interior. Trust status doesn't change the underlying value of the minerals, but it does change the process, the timeline, and sometimes the buyer pool, since not every buyer wants to work through BIA approval.

We're candid with owners that anyone quoting you a flat per-acre number sight unseen, before pulling your title or confirming trust status, is guessing. A real number depends on nearby well performance, whether your tract is fee or trust, and current royalty checks if you're already receiving them. We'll tell you plainly if we think your interest is worth more held than sold, particularly if there's active leasing interest nearby.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Big Horn County minerals are trust or fee?
faqs.a: Start at the Big Horn County Clerk and Recorder in Hardin for a title search on the recorded chain. If there's Crow allotment history in your family, the BIA Crow Agency realty office can confirm whether your specific interest is still held in trust or was patented out to fee status at some point.

faqs.q: Can trust minerals in the Crow Reservation be sold to a private buyer?
faqs.a: Often yes, but it requires BIA approval of the sale, and in many cases a valuation the BIA signs off on before the transaction can close. It's a longer process than a straight fee deed transfer, and not every prospective buyer is set up to work through it.

faqs.q: Is there active oil and gas drilling in Big Horn County right now?
faqs.a: The county sits on the quieter western flank of the Powder River Basin. There's legacy coalbed methane production and some older conventional wells, but nothing at the drilling pace you'd see in the Bakken counties farther east. Most owners here hold modest, aged, inherited interests rather than sitting under fresh permits.

faqs.q: What does a fair offer for Big Horn County mineral rights depend on?
faqs.a: Your recorded net revenue interest, whether the tract is fee or BIA trust, current or historical well performance nearby, and any active leasing activity in your section. We'd rather walk through your specific title and royalty history than quote a number before we've seen either.

faqs.q: Does the county clerk's office in Hardin handle trust mineral transfers?
faqs.a: The clerk and recorder handles fee-title recording, but trust interests are administered separately through the BIA. A courthouse title search will usually show whether the county has any record of the interest at all, which itself is a clue as to whether it's held in trust.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Carbon County, MT
items.meta: Mineral rights in Carbon County, MT near Red Lodge or Fromberg? A retired engineer explains the county's coal and Bighorn Basin oil history and honest offers.

sections.html:
Carbon County is a coal county first and an oil county second, and any offer on your minerals here should reflect that history honestly instead of pretending it's Bakken country.

Red Lodge is the county seat, and we always start there because the surrounding hills tell you what this county's mineral estate is actually built on. Carbon County was coal money before it was ever oil money, and the Smith Mine explosion outside Bearcreek in 1943, Montana's worst mining disaster, is still the reference point old-timers use when they talk about mineral rights here. That history matters because it shaped how land got patented, how surface and mineral estates got split, and how much of the county's oil and gas activity has stayed modest and conventional rather than turning into a shale boom.

The county straddles the north end of the Bighorn Basin, which gives it a genuinely different geologic identity than the Bakken counties on the eastern side of the state. If you own minerals near Fromberg, Bridger, Joliet, or Edgar, you're on the fringe of a basin that's produced conventional oil for a century in spots, mostly in small, structurally controlled fields rather than the resource-play drilling that gets headlines.

sections.title: Coal Legacy, Then Conventional Oil
sections.html:
The Bearcreek and Washoe coalfields anchored this county's economy through the first half of the last century, and a fair number of mineral estates here still carry coal reservations alongside oil and gas, layered from different eras of ownership. That layering matters at the courthouse. When we pull title on a Carbon County tract, we check whether the original severance split out coal separately from oil, gas, and other minerals, because it's not automatic and it affects exactly what you're being offered on.

On the oil side, the Elk Basin field straddles the Montana-Wyoming line near Fromberg and has produced since the early 1900s, one of the older conventional fields in this part of the Rockies. Production there and in smaller structures nearby has been in slow, managed decline for decades rather than fresh-drilled growth, which is a different value conversation than a county with active permitting.

sections.title: Bridger, Fromberg, Joliet, and the Beartooth Foothills
sections.html:
Bridger sits over its own small coalfield history and has seen scattered conventional oil interest tied to the same Bighorn Basin structural trend that runs through Fromberg. Joliet and Edgar, closer to the Yellowstone valley, have less oil and gas history and more ranch and irrigated farmland, with mineral ownership that in a lot of cases has never been actively developed at all, just carried on the deed since a homestead patent.

We tell owners in this part of the county not to assume dormant means worthless. An undeveloped or never-leased interest still has value if it sits in a spot a buyer thinks might see renewed interest, but it's a different kind of offer than one built off current production, and we'll say so plainly rather than dress it up.

sections.title: What Actually Moves an Offer Here
sections.html:
For producing or recently active tracts, we look at the well's decline history, whether the operator is current on royalty payments, and how your net revenue interest checks out against the recorded chain of title. For undeveloped tracts, the honest answer is that value is thinner and more speculative, tied more to proximity to the Elk Basin trend or renewed permitting than to any current cash flow.

We won't quote a flat per-acre figure for Carbon County minerals without seeing your specific tract, because a fractional interest under an actively producing well near Fromberg and a clean, undeveloped interest outside Joliet are not the same asset, even if they're both called mineral rights on paper.

faqs.q: Is Carbon County an active oil and gas drilling area?
faqs.a: Not in the way the Bakken counties are. Carbon County has a mix of legacy coal reservations and conventional oil production, mostly around the Elk Basin field near the Wyoming line, in slow decline rather than active new drilling.

faqs.q: Does your Carbon County mineral deed include coal rights?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A lot of older severances in this county split coal out separately from oil, gas, and other minerals, given the region's mining history. Pull the original severance deed at the Carbon County Clerk and Recorder in Red Lodge to see exactly what was reserved.

faqs.q: Your mineral interest near Joliet has never had a well on it. Is it worth anything?
faqs.a: It can still have value, but it's a speculative value tied to proximity to producing trends and future interest, not current royalty income. We'd rather give you an honest range for an undeveloped interest than imply it's worth what a producing tract nets.

faqs.q: What's the Elk Basin field and does it affect your minerals?
faqs.a: Elk Basin is a conventional oil field straddling the Montana-Wyoming border near Fromberg, producing since the early 1900s. If your tract sits near that trend, it's relevant to your value conversation even if your specific parcel has never been drilled.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Musselshell County, MT
items.meta: Own minerals under Bull Mountains coal or CBM acreage in Musselshell County? We buy fractional interests, heirship shares, and old family holdings around Roundup.

sections.html:
Musselshell County was a coal county before it was ever an oil county, and the mineral title here still shows it.

We spent enough years running production reports to know Musselshell County by its coal seams before its wellheads. The Bull Mountains coalfield sits under a good chunk of the county north and west of Roundup, and coalbed methane operators worked that acreage hard in the early 2000s. Some of that activity produced steady small royalty checks for a decade. A lot of it stalled out on water disposal costs and never got past the permitting stage. If you inherited an interest here, the deed probably reflects both eras — old homestead-era severances stacked under newer CBM leases that expired without ever spudding a well.

The other thing that shapes title in this county is the Northern Pacific land grant. The railroad got alternating sections across a wide corridor of central Montana in the 1860s, and that checkerboard pattern still runs through mineral ownership today. Two neighbors on adjoining quarter-sections can have completely different chains of title — one traces back to a homestead patent, the other to a railroad conveyance that reserved minerals separately. We don't guess at which pattern your parcel falls into. We pull the record.

sections.title: What's actually under the ground here
sections.html:
The Bull Mountains coal is thick, shallow, and easy to map, which is why CBM operators liked it on paper. Water production out of those coal seams was the problem — a lot of it, and expensive to handle, which is why the play never scaled the way the Powder River Basin did across the state line in Wyoming. There's also scattered conventional oil and gas activity in the county tied to smaller structural traps, but nothing that ever built into a sustained field the way the Bakken counties did on the eastern edge of the state.

That matters for what your interest is worth today. A Musselshell County mineral interest tends to be judged less on current cash flow and more on whether it sits inside a defined CBM unit with a still-active operator, or whether the lease that once covered it has lapsed. We look at both before we ever put a number in front of you.

sections.title: Heirship and colony land
sections.html:
This county has more Hutterite colony land than most people outside Montana realize, and colony-held minerals get administered differently than a typical family parcel — often as a communal interest rather than individual fractional shares. Separately, a lot of the old homestead-era mineral severances around Roundup, Melstone, and Musselshell have passed through two or three generations without ever being formally probated. We run into five, six, sometimes a dozen heirs holding a single quarter-section interest, most of them living outside Montana and unaware anyone else in the family still holds a piece.

If that's your situation, the clerk and recorder's office in Roundup is where we start — pulling the patent, the severance deed, and every conveyance since to build a clean chain before we make an offer. We'd rather spend the time up front than hand you a number we can't stand behind.

sections.title: Leasing history and what a lapsed lease means
sections.html:
Most of the CBM leasing in this county happened between roughly 2001 and 2008. A lot of those leases had short primary terms and shut-in clauses that let the operator hold acreage without producing much. When gas prices fell and water handling costs stayed high, plenty of that leased ground reverted back to the mineral owner with nothing ever drilled. If your family's interest was leased in that window and you haven't seen a bonus or delay rental payment since, there's a decent chance the lease has expired and the minerals are open again.

An open, unleased interest and a held-by-production interest are two different assets with two different values, and we'll tell you plainly which one you're holding before we talk numbers.

sections.title: How we evaluate a Musselshell County interest
sections.html:
We start with the legal description and county records, then check whether the parcel sits inside an active CBM spacing unit, a lapsed leasehold, or unleased ground with no recent activity. We look at production history if there is any, decline behavior on nearby wells, and whether any operator has permitted activity on or near the tract in the last few years. Values here vary a lot depending on those factors — an interest in an active unit with a producing well can be worth meaningfully more than an identical-sized interest in ground that's been idle for a decade, so we won't quote a flat number without doing that work first.

We buy fractional interests of any size, including small heir shares that most buyers skip because the paperwork takes longer than the check is worth. That's fine with us — we do the title work ourselves.

faqs.q: Is there active oil or gas production in Musselshell County right now?
faqs.a: Some, tied mostly to the Bull Mountains CBM acreage and scattered conventional wells, but the county has never had a sustained boom like the Bakken counties to the east. Activity varies by section, which is why we check the specific parcel rather than the county as a whole.

faqs.q: Your family's minerals are held by a Hutterite colony — can you still buy an interest?
faqs.a: It depends on how the colony holds title. Communal colony land is administered differently than individual heir interests, and we'll need to see how your family's original conveyance was structured before we can tell you what's possible.

faqs.q: The lease on your minerals expired years ago — does that change the value?
faqs.a: Yes, in both directions. An unleased interest has more optionality but no current cash flow. We'll tell you which situation you're in before quoting anything.

faqs.q: Do you need to go to the courthouse in Roundup yourself?
faqs.a: No. We pull the recorded documents directly from the Musselshell County Clerk and Recorder as part of our own due diligence before making an offer.

faqs.q: What if your interest is a small fractional share from an old homestead?
faqs.a: Those are common in this county and we buy them regularly. Small doesn't mean worthless, and it doesn't mean we'll skip the title work either.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Wibaux County, MT
items.meta: Own minerals in Wibaux County, Montana? An ex-E&P engineer explains the Cedar Creek Anticline, split estate, and what a fair offer looks like on the Bakken's edge.

sections.html:
Wibaux County sits on the edge of two different stories, not the middle of one, and that changes what your minerals are actually worth.

Wibaux County is about as far east as Montana gets, the county seat of the same name sitting a few miles off the North Dakota line along I-94. Ask most landmen about Montana's oil counties and they'll point you to Richland or Sheridan County, further south along the Williston Basin's better rock. Wibaux gets mentioned almost as an afterthought, and that's honestly closer to the truth than the marketing some buyers will feed you.

We spent a career running production on the North Dakota side of this line, and crossing into Wibaux County always felt like stepping off the edge of the map. The Bakken and Three Forks are still down there, but they thin and get less economic the further west you go. What's actually kept this county producing for decades is older, shallower, and less talked about: the Cedar Creek Anticline.

sections.title: The Cedar Creek Anticline, Not the Bakken Fairway
sections.html:
The Cedar Creek Anticline is a long structural fold running northwest to southeast through Fallon, Wibaux, and Dawson counties before it dips into North Dakota. Fields like Pennel and Cabin Creek were found on it back in the 1950s and 1960s, producing out of the Charles Formation and Red River dolomite rather than the Bakken shale you hear about further east. Those wells decline slow and produce small, and a lot of them are still on the pump today, just at a fraction of their original rates.

If someone's offering to buy your Wibaux County minerals on the strength of a Bakken horizontal two counties over, ask them which formation their comparable actually came out of. A Cedar Creek Anticline royalty check and a Three Forks horizontal royalty check are built on completely different decline curves, and pricing one off the other is how sellers get shorted.

sections.title: Split Estate from the Homestead Years
sections.html:
This county filled in with dryland wheat and cattle operations under the Enlarged Homestead Act in the 1910s, and a lot of those original patents either reserved minerals to the homesteader or, in the case of Stock-Raising Homestead Act parcels after 1916, reserved them to the federal government instead. A century later, the surface owner running cattle on a Wibaux County section and the family holding the mineral certificate underneath it are often not the same people, and sometimes one of those tracts is federal minerals under a BLM lease rather than fee minerals under a private lease.

Figuring out which situation you're in matters more than any number a buyer quotes you up front. Fee minerals and federal minerals get valued, leased, and transferred through different processes entirely.

sections.title: What the Royalty Check Actually Tells You
sections.html:
If you're getting a statement off a Cedar Creek Anticline well, expect a decline curve that's already flattened out, older wells that produce modestly and steadily rather than the sharp first-year drop-off you'd see from a new horizontal further east. That steadiness is worth something to a buyer even without headline volumes, since it's a more predictable cash flow than a young Bakken well still working through its decline.

Any value talk should be tied to what's actually on your division order and JIB statement, deducts and all, not to a per-acre figure someone read off a Richland County deal. Your gross production tax rate, your net revenue interest, and the well's current decline stage are what a real offer gets built from.

sections.title: Running Title from the Wibaux County Courthouse
sections.html:
The Wibaux County Clerk and Recorder's office holds the deed and patent chain for most of these parcels, and because the county's small, that office doesn't have the staff or the digitized backlog that a bigger county does. Title work here often means tracing a chain back to the original homestead patent by hand, which takes longer than folks expect when they're first trying to sell.

If your family's mineral interest has been sitting untouched since a grandparent or great-uncle passed, budget real time for a title company or landman to run that chain before any closing happens. It's not unusual for a Wibaux County parcel to need probate cleanup two or three generations back before a deed can transfer cleanly.

faqs.q: Do you own your minerals if you own the surface in Wibaux County?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Between Enlarged Homestead and Stock-Raising Homestead patents, a lot of surface and mineral estates split apart a century ago. Some of the county is federal (BLM-administered) minerals rather than fee minerals, so check your deed and patent history before assuming.

faqs.q: What's a Cedar Creek Anticline royalty check usually worth compared to Bakken counties?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on the specific well's decline stage and your net revenue interest, but Cedar Creek Anticline wells are generally older and lower-volume than newer Bakken horizontals further east. Value should track your actual statement, not a per-acre number from a different play.

faqs.q: How do you find your mineral deed if your family left Wibaux County decades ago?
faqs.a: Start with the Wibaux County Clerk and Recorder's office for the deed and patent chain. If there's been a death in the ownership line without a probate filed, expect that to add time before any sale or lease can close cleanly.

faqs.q: Should you sell now or hold on the Bakken's western edge?
faqs.a: That depends on your own cash needs, the well's decline stage, and how many heirs are involved in the interest, not on a blanket rule for the county. Ask for the specifics behind any offer rather than a flat yes or no.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Wibaux County parcel is federal or fee minerals?
faqs.a: Your patent history will show it. If the original homestead patent falls after the 1916 Stock-Raising Homestead Act and reserved minerals to the United States, that tract is federal minerals under BLM administration, leased differently than fee minerals a title company can transfer directly.

sections.title: Geology on the Powder River Basin's Western Rim
sections.html: Big Horn County sits on the far western edge of the Powder River Basin, where coalbed methane development in the late 1990s and 2000s put wells into the Fort Union coal seams. That activity has slowed considerably from its peak, and most producing interests near Hardin today are aged, in steady decline, rather than freshly drilled. There's no meaningful deep shale activity here comparable to the Bakken counties on the state's other side.

sections.title: The Poplar Field, Not a Fresh Bakken Horizontal

sections.title: Working Through BIA Approval Without Losing Momentum

Red Lodge sits on the old Rocky Fork coalfield, and the mining that built this town ended the way a lot of Montana coal country ended — gradually through the 1930s and 40s, and then abruptly, after the Smith Mine disaster in 1943 killed 74 men and effectively closed the district for good within a few years. If your family's mineral interest near Red Lodge traces back to that era, the deed history is often coal-specific, severed separately from any oil and gas rights under the same ground, sometimes generations apart.

Oil and gas activity in the immediate Red Lodge area itself has been minor — the county's real conventional oil history sits further north and east, around the Elk Basin field near Bridger and Fromberg. We don't conflate the two when we evaluate an interest here.

sections.title: Coal rights versus oil and gas rights

faqs.q: Is your family's Red Lodge mineral interest coal or oil and gas?
