items.meta: Plentywood is Sheridan County's seat, on the thinner edge of the Bakken. We buy mineral interests here, priced against real production, not ND-core hype.

sections.html:
Plentywood is the courthouse town for the whole county, and it's also where we start every title search on a Sheridan County interest, no matter which small town the family calls from.

Of everywhere in Sheridan County, Plentywood has seen the most consistent Bakken-era activity, closer to the play's stronger extension than the ground further west toward the Saskatchewan line. That said, we want to be straight with anyone calling from here: consistent activity in an edge county still means thinner net pay and lower well density than the North Dakota core, and the royalty checks reflect that difference. We evaluate your interest against its actual production record, not against what the county courthouse gossip says about the boom years.

Being the county seat also means Plentywood is where every other town's title work eventually routes through, so we know this record about as well as any in the county.

sections.title: What we check first for a Plentywood-area interest
sections.html: We pull the recorded chain from the Sheridan County Clerk and Recorder right here in town, confirm whether the interest is currently leased or unleased, and check nearby well production and decline. Plentywood-area interests are more likely than most in the county to have an active lease on file, but that doesn't mean every parcel does.

sections.title: Older conventional layers under the newer leases
sections.html: This county had conventional Madison-formation production decades before the Bakken boom, and some of that older leasing history still shows up in the record around Plentywood. We check for both eras rather than assuming your family's interest is purely a Bakken-era story.

faqs.q: Is Plentywood the most active part of Sheridan County?
faqs.a: Generally yes, relative to the rest of the county, though still on the thinner western edge of the Bakken compared to North Dakota core acreage.

faqs.q: Where do you pull the deed records for Plentywood-area interests?
faqs.a: Directly from the Sheridan County Clerk and Recorder here in town — we don't ask you to track it down.

faqs.q: Could your family's old lease be from before the Bakken boom?
faqs.a: Possibly, if it traces to the 1950s or 60s conventional Madison production era. We check the full record before quoting.

faqs.q: Why does being the county seat matter for your title search?
faqs.a: It doesn't change your parcel's value, but it does mean we're already deeply familiar with the record system we'll be pulling your documents from.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Culbertson, MT
items.meta: Culbertson, MT sits near the Missouri River in Roosevelt County, close to the Bakken's Montana edge. A retired engineer explains title, trust land, and offers.

sections.html:
Culbertson has more actual drilling history nearby than most towns on this list, which means the title work matters even more, not less.

Culbertson sits along the Missouri River in eastern Roosevelt County, close enough to the North Dakota line that Bakken activity has reached into this area more consistently than in the county's western reaches. That's good news for value, but it also means more people are asking about title, more wells have been drilled and re-drilled, and more division orders have been amended over the years. Getting the current numbers right matters.

sections.title: Real Activity, Real Complexity
sections.html: Where the play has actually reached Culbertson-area sections, we've seen operators drill multiple horizontal wells targeting both the Bakken and the underlying Three Forks bench from a single pad, which means a single mineral tract can end up with interests in several distinct units over time. If you're already receiving royalty checks, comparing your most recent division order against your original lease is worth doing before any sale conversation, because pooled unit percentages shift as new wells come online.

sections.title: Fort Peck Reservation Boundary Nearby
sections.html: Culbertson itself sits outside the Fort Peck Reservation boundary in most mapping, but Roosevelt County overall has substantial reservation acreage, and tracts just outside town can still be affected depending on the exact parcel. We always confirm fee versus trust status early, because it's a five-minute question at the courthouse that saves weeks of confusion later.

sections.title: What Drives Value on an Active Tract
sections.html: For a producing interest near Culbertson, we look at how many wells are actually on your unit, current production decline, whether the operator is current on payments, and any newer permits that suggest additional drilling. This is genuinely one of the stronger corners of the Bakken MT footprint, and we'll say so directly rather than undersell an area that has real production behind it.

faqs.q: How active is Bakken drilling near Culbertson, MT?
faqs.a: More active than most of the Montana side of the play, given the proximity to the North Dakota core. Multi-well pads targeting both the Bakken and Three Forks are common in productive sections nearby.

faqs.q: Why did your royalty percentage change on an older lease near Culbertson?
faqs.a: As additional wells get drilled into a pooled unit, your net revenue interest is recalculated against the new unit configuration. Comparing your current division order to your original lease will show exactly what changed and why.

faqs.q: Is land near Culbertson inside the Fort Peck Reservation?
faqs.a: Most of the town itself sits outside the reservation boundary, but Roosevelt County has significant reservation acreage overall. Confirm your specific parcel's status at the Roosevelt County Clerk and Recorder in Wolf Point before assuming either way.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Fairview, MT
items.meta: Fairview sits on the Montana-North Dakota line in Richland County, near real Bakken production. A retired engineer explains cross-border units before selling.

sections.html:
Fairview straddles the state line closely enough that some of the mineral units touching this town cross into North Dakota, which is a wrinkle worth understanding before you sell.

Richland County's eastern edge, where Fairview sits, is genuinely productive Bakken territory, benefiting both from proximity to the original Elm Coulee discovery area and from spillover activity out of the more intensively drilled McKenzie County core just across the North Dakota border. We treat this as one of the stronger positions in the Bakken MT footprint, with the caveat that cross-border units add a layer of complexity to the paperwork.

sections.title: Cross-Border Unit Realities
sections.html: When a spacing unit straddles the state line, the operator has to deal with two states' regulatory frameworks and, in some cases, two counties' recording requirements. If your Fairview-area interest sits in one of these units, your division order should reflect exactly how much of the unit falls in Montana versus North Dakota, and that split affects your actual net revenue interest. We always confirm this directly rather than assume a unit is entirely on one side of the line.

sections.title: Production History Worth Checking
sections.html: This part of Richland County has seen consistent horizontal drilling activity since the mid-2000s, targeting both the Bakken and Three Forks. Wells here often show solid early production followed by the steady decline typical of the play, and multiple wells per unit are common where operators have come back to develop the Three Forks bench separately from the original Bakken well.

sections.title: Evaluating a Fairview-Area Interest
sections.html: We look at how many wells are actually producing from your unit, current decline trends, and whether any part of your interest crosses into North Dakota. Given the strength of this position within the Bakken MT footprint, we'd expect a fair offer here to reflect genuinely active production rather than flank-county caution.

faqs.q: Does your mineral interest near Fairview cross into North Dakota?
faqs.a: It's possible, given the town's position right on the state line. Your division order should specify the exact unit boundaries. If it doesn't clearly state this, a title check at the Richland County Clerk and Recorder in Sidney can confirm it.

faqs.q: Is Fairview, MT a strong area for mineral value?
faqs.a: Relative to most of the Bakken MT footprint, yes. This part of Richland County has consistent horizontal drilling history and benefits from proximity to both Elm Coulee and the more active North Dakota core.

faqs.q: Why might there be more than one well on your unit?
faqs.a: Operators often drill an initial Bakken well and later come back to develop the Three Forks bench beneath it as a separate well in the same unit. Each additional well can affect your calculated net revenue interest.

faqs.q: Why do neighboring Savage parcels sometimes have such different values?

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Bainville, MT
items.meta: Bainville sits right on the North Dakota line in Roosevelt County. A retired E&P engineer explains what that border position means for Bakken activity and mineral offers here.

sections.html:
Bainville is close enough to McKenzie County, North Dakota that we check both sides of the line before we'll say anything about a tract's value here.

Roosevelt County's eastern edge, where Bainville sits, is about as close as Montana gets to the true Bakken core across the border. That proximity matters, but it's not automatic. We've worked plenty of Roosevelt County tracts that see real leasing interest and plenty a few miles away that don't, so we'd rather look at your specific section than assume border proximity alone tells the story.

sections.title: Border-County Geology
sections.html: The Bakken and Three Forks formations run continuously across the state line, and pay quality near Bainville can be meaningfully better than in counties farther west in Montana, simply because you're closer to the thicker, more consistently productive part of the play centered around McKenzie and Williams Counties in North Dakota. Operators active on the North Dakota side have, at times, pushed units across the line into eastern Roosevelt County, so checking current permitting near your specific tract is worth the effort.

sections.title: Fort Peck Reservation Overlap
sections.html: Roosevelt County includes a significant portion of the Fort Peck Indian Reservation, home to the Assiniboine and Sioux Tribes. Depending on exactly where your tract sits and its ownership history, your interest could be fee, allotted trust land administered through the BIA, or tribal. That distinction changes the sale process meaningfully, since trust interests require BIA approval rather than a straightforward deed transfer, so we always ask about this before quoting anything.

sections.title: Evaluating a Bainville-Area Interest
sections.html: We look at recent permitting activity on the North Dakota side near the state line, confirm whether your interest is fee or trust, and pull your recorded net revenue interest against the current division order if a well is already producing. Given the border position, this is one of the more active corners of the Bakken MT footprint, but we still won't quote you a number without seeing the actual title.

faqs.q: Is Bainville, MT in the core Bakken play?
faqs.a: It's close to the core, being right on the North Dakota border near McKenzie County, but Montana-side pay quality still tends to run thinner than the North Dakota core. It's a stronger position than the rest of the Bakken MT footprint, not identical to it.

faqs.q: How do you know if your mineral interest near Bainville is trust or fee land?
faqs.a: Roosevelt County includes part of the Fort Peck Reservation, so trust status is a real possibility. Check the Roosevelt County Clerk and Recorder in Wolf Point first, and if there's any tribal allotment history in your family, follow up with the BIA Fort Peck Agency.

faqs.q: Does an operator have to be actively drilling for your interest to have value?
faqs.a: No, but current permitting nearby, especially on the North Dakota side of the line near Bainville, is a meaningful factor. We'd check recent activity in your specific section before quoting a range.

If activity has moved this direction recently, that changes the conversation, and we'll walk through exactly what we found before naming a number.

faqs.q: Is there active drilling near Froid, MT?

faqs.q: How do you find your recorded mineral interest percentage near Froid?
faqs.a: The Roosevelt County Clerk and Recorder in Wolf Point holds the recorded deeds and, if applicable, division orders for producing tracts. That's the starting point for confirming exactly what you hold.

faqs.q: Should you sell an undeveloped interest near Froid or wait?

Reserve sits up near the Saskatchewan line, about as far north as Sheridan County reaches, and the mineral record here is as quiet as the drive up to it.

The Bakken does extend north across the border into Saskatchewan, which surprises some Reserve-area families who assume the play stops at the international line. It doesn't, geologically, but the economics on this side of the border in far northern Sheridan County have never supported the kind of development seen closer to the North Dakota core. Most interests we run into near Reserve are quiet, unleased, homestead-era holdings, and we evaluate them as exactly that.

We mention the Saskatchewan extension because it's genuinely interesting geology, not because it changes what we can offer for ground on this side of the line today.

sections.title: Basin edge meets international edge
sections.html: Reserve sits at a genuine double edge — the western flank of the Bakken and the northern edge of the play near the border. Both factors point the same direction: thinner pay, less drilling incentive, and a quieter lease history than counties further south and east. We don't dress that up when we talk to a family here.

faqs.q: Is a quiet, unleased interest near Reserve still worth calling about?

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Wibaux, MT
items.meta: Own minerals near Wibaux, Montana? A retired E&P engineer explains the Cedar Creek Anticline, split estate from the cattle-baron era, and honest offer math.

sections.html:
Wibaux was cattle country before it was oil country, and the town's own name comes from that history.

The town of Wibaux takes its name from Pierre Wibaux, a French cattleman who ran one of the biggest outfits in eastern Montana back in the 1880s, and the county seat still carries that ranching identity more than any drilling one. Sit at the courthouse a while and you'll hear more about cattle prices than crude, which tells you something honest about where this town's minerals actually sit.

sections.title: Same Trend as the County, Same Honest Story
sections.html: Wibaux sits right along the Cedar Creek Anticline, the older structural trend that's produced modestly out of the Charles Formation and Red River dolomite for decades. That's different rock and a different decline curve than the Bakken shale further east in North Dakota, and any offer on your Wibaux-area minerals should be priced off that older, slower profile rather than a headline Williston number.

sections.title: Small Town, Scattered Ownership
sections.html: In a town this size, everybody's grandparents knew everybody else's grandparents, and mineral interests here often trace back to the same handful of original ranch and homestead families. That familiarity doesn't make title simpler though. It's common for a Wibaux mineral certificate to have split among siblings or cousins two or three generations back, with some of those heirs long gone from the area.

sections.title: What to Ask Before You Sign Anything
sections.html: Before you take a number from anyone, ask which well or unit their offer is based on, what your current net revenue interest is, and whether your tract is fee minerals or falls under a federal reservation from the homestead era. A fair buyer will walk through that with you instead of quoting a flat per-acre figure and hoping you don't ask questions.

faqs.q: Is Wibaux part of the core Bakken play?
faqs.a: No. Wibaux sits on the Bakken's western fringe where the shale thins out. Most local production comes from the older Cedar Creek Anticline trend instead, with a slower, steadier decline curve than a Bakken horizontal.

faqs.q: Where do you record or research a mineral deed near Wibaux?
faqs.a: The Wibaux County Clerk and Recorder's office handles deed and patent records for the town and surrounding sections. Being a small county, expect title research to take real time, especially for older heirship interests.

faqs.q: Does being close to North Dakota make your Wibaux minerals worth more?
faqs.a: Proximity alone doesn't set value, the producing formation and well economics do. A Cedar Creek Anticline interest near Wibaux is priced differently than a Bakken interest just across the state line, even a short drive apart.

Billings is a downstream and midstream hub, refineries and pipelines, not necessarily a center of upstream drilling in the immediate area.

sections.title: Refining Hub, Not Necessarily Drilling Ground
sections.html: The Billings area has hosted refineries for decades, processing crude that arrives by pipeline from producing areas elsewhere in Montana, Wyoming, and Canada. That infrastructure is real and valuable to the regional economy, but it doesn't mean the ground directly under Acton or nearby Yellowstone County farmland has equivalent drilling activity. We check actual well and permit records for the specific area rather than assume refinery proximity implies local production.

sections.title: What Ownership Typically Looks Like Here

Fractional interests split among multiple heirs are common, and confirming the exact recorded percentage is usually the necessary first step before any value conversation.

That double history is exactly why we don't shortcut the title work here. Two Silesia-area parcels a half-mile apart can carry completely different mineral pictures depending on which era the original severance dates to.

sections.title: Elk Basin's long, slow decline
sections.html: Elk Basin has been producing for more than a hundred years, which sounds impressive until you understand what stripper-well decline actually looks like this late in a field's life — low, steady volumes, thin margins for the operator, and royalty checks that reflect that reality rather than boom-era numbers. If your interest touches this field, we evaluate it against current decline curves, not against what an old family story says it was worth decades ago.

sections.title: Coal-era severances layered underneath
sections.html: Because this ground was coal country before it was oil country, we check whether your deed reserved coal rights, oil and gas rights, or both, and whether those rights were later split apart in a separate conveyance. It's a common enough pattern here that we never assume.

faqs.q: Does your interest near Silesia touch the Elk Basin field?
faqs.a: Possibly — it depends on your exact legal description. We check that against the field's current boundary and any active units before quoting.

faqs.q: Elk Basin has been producing since 1915 — is your interest worth a lot?
faqs.a: Age doesn't equal value this late in a field's life. Elk Basin is in long stripper-well decline, and we price interests against current production, not the field's history.

faqs.q: Could your family's deed be coal rights instead of oil and gas?
faqs.a: It's possible given the area's coal-camp history. We read the actual deed language to confirm what you hold before making an offer.

faqs.q: Who holds the county records for a Silesia-area parcel?
faqs.a: The Carbon County Clerk and Recorder in Red Lodge. We pull the chain directly rather than relying on family recollection of the original severance.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in St. Xavier, MT
items.meta: St. Xavier, MT sits along the Bighorn River on Crow Reservation land near Bighorn Canyon. We buy trust and fee mineral interests here based on real records.

sections.html:
St. Xavier sits along the Bighorn River toward the southern end of the reservation, closer to Bighorn Canyon than to any active drilling.

This is quiet ground on the mineral side. The coalbed methane activity that touched parts of the Crow Reservation to the north and east never reached this far south in any meaningful way, and most St. Xavier-area interests we encounter have no recent lease or production history. What we do check carefully, every time, is land status — whether the interest is trust land requiring BIA approval to sell, or fee land that moves through the standard county process — because that question matters here regardless of how quiet the production picture is.

The Bighorn Canyon country nearby draws visitors for the scenery, not for any mineral activity, and we don't let that confuse the actual record we're working from.

sections.title: Confirming land status before anything else
sections.html: We don't guess on this. We check BIA records for trust status and the Big Horn County Clerk and Recorder in Hardin for fee land, and we explain to the family which process applies before we discuss value at all.

sections.title: Pricing quiet river-country ground honestly
sections.html: Without production or lease history, we price a St. Xavier-area interest as long-term potential, not current income, and we're clear about what that means so there's no confusion about the number.

sections.title: Why we still take these calls seriously
sections.html: A quiet record doesn't mean we rush the process. We verify the legal description and land status with the same care we'd give a parcel sitting inside an active CBM unit, because getting it right matters regardless of how much activity is nearby.

faqs.q: Is there any oil or gas activity near St. Xavier?
faqs.a: Very little on record. Coalbed methane development elsewhere on the reservation never extended significantly this far south.

faqs.q: How do you confirm whether your interest is trust or fee land?
faqs.a: We check both BIA and Big Horn County records directly using your family name and rough parcel description.

faqs.q: Is it worth selling an interest that's never produced anything?
faqs.a: For some families, yes, priced as long-term potential. We'll walk through the reasoning honestly before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does proximity to Bighorn Canyon affect mineral value?
faqs.a: No. Scenic or recreational significance doesn't factor into subsurface mineral value — we price the interest on lease and production history alone.

faqs.q: Do you take small or quiet St. Xavier-area interests as seriously as active ones?
faqs.a: Yes. We verify the legal description and land status with the same care regardless of how much production history exists.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Worden, MT
items.meta: Worden sits in irrigated Yellowstone County farm country, not a drilling hotspot. An ex-E&P engineer explains what's realistically under your land.

sections.html:
Worden's history is about water, not oil, and that's the honest starting point for anyone asking what their minerals here are worth.

Worden sits along the Yellowstone River in the stretch of Yellowstone County settled through the old Huntley Project, one of the Bureau of Reclamation's early 1900s irrigation efforts that turned this bottomland into sugar beet and hay ground. It's productive farm country, but it was never a drilling destination, and it still isn't.

We get calls from folks around Worden and neighboring Ballantine and Huntley who assume that because the county seat in Billings has refineries, there must be something worth drilling under their own quarter section too. Usually there isn't, and we'd rather tell you that upfront than let a slick offer letter convince you otherwise.

sections.title: Irrigated Ground Over Quiet Minerals
sections.html:
When the Huntley Project brought canals through this area, the attention went to water rights, not mineral rights, and that priority has basically held for over a century. Most Worden-area landowners never had reason to think much about what was reserved or conveyed underground when the land changed hands generation to generation.

That's part of why so many current owners around Worden don't actually know their own mineral status. A deed passed down through a farm sale or an estate settlement rarely spelled out mineral reservations clearly, so the honest first step is confirming what you have before worrying about what it's worth.

sections.title: What's Realistically Down There
sections.html:
Yellowstone County has a handful of small, older conventional pools scattered around its edges, but nothing of consequence sits directly under Worden itself. If you're holding a mineral interest here, the honest expectation is low current activity rather than an active unit waiting to be drilled.

That doesn't mean the interest is worthless, it means it should be priced like what it is: an undeveloped position in a quiet corner of the county rather than a working royalty.

sections.title: Why a Buyer Would Still Want It
sections.html:
Interests like this get bought for the long view, not a quick payout, on the chance that basin-wide interest or a nearby permit eventually changes the picture. If someone approaches you with an offer, ask what specifically they're basing it on, since there's rarely a producing well nearby to point to.

A buyer working this kind of ground is usually assembling a larger position across several Yellowstone County tracts rather than chasing your parcel alone, and that context is worth asking about directly.

faqs.q: Is there active drilling near Worden?
faqs.a: No, not currently. Worden sits in irrigated farm country within Yellowstone County, and there's no producing activity directly beneath the town or its immediate surroundings.

faqs.q: Why would anyone buy minerals here if there's no drilling?
faqs.a: Some buyers hold undeveloped interests on a long timeline, betting that future basin-wide activity or a nearby permit could eventually change the picture. It's speculative, not a near-term payout.

faqs.q: How do you know if you even have mineral rights under your Worden land?
faqs.a: Check your deed and the original patent chain through the Yellowstone County Clerk and Recorder's office. Irrigation-era conveyances didn't always handle mineral reservations the same way dryland homestead patents did, so it's worth confirming rather than assuming.

faqs.q: Is a Worden-area mineral interest worth anything to sell?
faqs.a: It can be, but expect a modest, speculative valuation rather than a producing-royalty price, since there's no active well backing it. A buyer here is paying for long-term potential, not current cash flow.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Wyola, MT
items.meta: Wyola sits on the Powder River Basin's Montana edge, near Crow Reservation trust land. A retired E&P engineer explains what that means for a sale.

sections.html:
Wyola is Montana's edge of a Wyoming play, and that geography, plus reservation status, decides more about your minerals than any national headline does.

Wyola sits just off I-90 near the Wyoming line, close enough to Sheridan that most of the regional oilfield traffic passes through on its way to somewhere else. It's also within the Crow Reservation, which means ownership status matters here as much as geology does.

sections.title: The Powder River Basin's Thin Montana Edge
sections.html: The Powder River Basin's coalbed methane boom of the 2000s reached into Big Horn and Rosebud counties, pulling gas from the Fort Union coal seams alongside a lot of produced water that had to be managed. That activity was always thinner and more marginal on the Montana side than in the basin's Wyoming core around Gillette, and it slowed well before the newer horizontal plays further south ever got going. Anyone comparing a Wyola interest to Wyoming numbers is comparing it to the wrong play.

sections.title: Crow Reservation Trust and Allotted Minerals
sections.html: Ownership near Wyola often traces back to Crow Tribe allotments, and those interests can carry trust or restricted status requiring Bureau of Indian Affairs approval to transfer, distinct from fee minerals that move by standard deed. Checkerboard ownership is common here too, where a fee tract and a trust tract sit right next to each other with completely different transfer rules.

sections.title: Reading an Offer on Wyola Minerals
sections.html: A fair offer here should reference the older CBM history and current decline rather than newer Wyoming-side numbers, and it should tell you upfront whether your interest needs BIA sign-off. If a buyer skips both of those and just names a number, ask them to show their work.

faqs.q: Is Wyola in the same play as Gillette, Wyoming?
faqs.a: It's the same basin but a much thinner, older edge of it. The Powder River Basin's core activity around Gillette has always outpaced the Montana side near Wyola, so pricing shouldn't be borrowed directly from Wyoming comparables.

faqs.q: Are your minerals trust or fee near Wyola?
faqs.a: Check your deed and allotment history. Many interests here trace to Crow Tribe allotments and may require Bureau of Indian Affairs approval to transfer, while neighboring fee tracts do not.

faqs.q: Why did coalbed methane activity slow down here?
faqs.a: The Montana side of the Powder River Basin was always more marginal than the Wyoming core, and as gas prices and water-handling costs shifted, operators focused their capital on the more productive Wyoming acreage instead.

situations.title: Owner Situations

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Just inherited Montana mineral rights? A former E&P engineer explains what to check first, how to value the interest, and when keeping versus selling actually makes sense.

sections.html:
You inherited a paper interest in something you've probably never seen, ground you may never have visited, tied to a well you didn't know existed until the letter arrived.

Inheriting mineral rights in Montana usually starts with confusion, not clarity. Maybe a parent or grandparent mentioned minerals once, decades ago, and then it never came up again until a probate attorney handed you a stack of paperwork or a small royalty check showed up with no explanation. That's normal. A lot of Montana mineral ownership sat quiet for generations before anything got drilled nearby, and heirs often have no real sense of whether what they inherited is worth keeping, selling, or just filing away.

The first job isn't deciding whether to sell. It's figuring out what you actually own, whether it's producing, and whether the county and legal description even match what you think they do. Everything after that gets easier.

sections.title: Start with the paperwork, not a guess
sections.html:
If the estate went through probate, there should be a decree of distribution or similar document identifying the specific mineral interest and its legal description. If there's also a division order, either in the deceased's name or already transferred to you, that tells you the operator, the well, and your exact decimal interest. Without those documents, the county clerk and recorder's office where the minerals sit can usually help you trace the chain of title, though it can take some legwork if the original deed is old.

We ask every inheriting owner the same first questions: what county, is there a division order, and has a royalty check ever actually arrived. The answers usually tell us within a few minutes whether we're talking about a producing interest, a leased-but-undrilled interest, or something dormant that hasn't seen activity in years, and each of those gets valued differently.

sections.title: Keeping the interest: what that actually means long-term
sections.html:
Keeping inherited minerals means staying on the hook for tracking royalty statements, filing them at tax time, responding to lease renewal offers, and eventually passing the interest down to your own heirs, possibly fractionalizing it further in the process. For some owners, especially those with a meaningful producing interest and a connection to the family land, that ongoing role is worth it. For others, particularly heirs who live out of state or inherited a small piece of a larger family holding, it becomes one more thing to manage for income that may not be large enough to justify the hassle.

There's no universally right answer here. We'd rather walk you through what the interest is actually paying, and what it's realistically worth if sold, than tell you which choice is correct. That's your call to make with real numbers in front of you.

sections.title: Selling: what changes and what doesn't
sections.html:
Selling an inherited interest converts an uncertain, sometimes confusing asset into a single, known amount, useful if the estate needs to be settled among multiple heirs, if you'd rather not deal with an asset tied to land you've never visited, or if you simply want the certainty of cash over decades of unpredictable royalty checks. It doesn't erase the history of the land or your family's connection to it, that stays regardless of who owns the minerals going forward.

Depending on how the interest is producing and where it sits relative to current drilling activity, a fair offer typically gets built from recent royalty history if there is any, or from lease and permitting activity nearby if there isn't.

sections.title: Getting an inherited interest reviewed
sections.html: Gather whatever probate documents, division orders, or old royalty statements you have, even partial or old ones help, and send them over. We'll tell you plainly what you're looking at, what it's likely worth, and whether we think it makes more sense to hold or sell given your specific situation, no pressure either direction.

faqs.q: You inherited minerals but have never received a royalty check. Are they worth anything?
faqs.a: Possibly, and it depends on whether there's an active lease, nearby drilling, or historical production that stopped. Non-producing minerals aren't automatically worthless, but they get valued differently than a currently producing interest.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to transfer the mineral interest into your name before selling?
faqs.a: If the estate hasn't been fully probated or the deed hasn't been updated to reflect your ownership, that typically needs to happen before a sale can close cleanly. We can point you toward what's usually needed, though the legal work itself should go through an attorney or the probate process in your county.

faqs.q: Multiple siblings inherited the same interest. Do you all have to agree to sell?
faqs.a: Each heir typically owns their own undivided share and can generally sell their own portion independently, though it's worth coordinating so everyone understands the process and nobody's caught off guard by a new co-owner.

faqs.q: How do you find out what county your inherited minerals are actually in?
faqs.a: The probate decree or original deed should list a legal description including county, township, and section. If you're missing that document, the county clerk's office where you believe the family land was located can often help trace it.

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: A mailer showed up quoting a price for your Montana minerals. A retired operator explains how to check whether it's fair before signing anything back.

sections.html:
A letter shows up quoting a number for minerals you may have forgotten you owned, and the pressure to just sign and mail it back is real. Slow down for a week; it costs you nothing.

Unsolicited mineral offers are a real part of this business, and not all of them are bad faith. Some come from legitimate buyers who pull county records, see production or lease activity, and mail out standard offers to owners of record. Others are built to look official while quoting well under what the interest is worth, betting that most owners won't check. From the outside, both look almost identical: a letter with a dollar figure, a deed for you to sign, and often a deadline creating urgency.

The single best thing you can do with any unsolicited offer is treat the number as a starting point for questions, not a final answer. A legitimate offer holds up to scrutiny. One that doesn't want to be checked usually isn't a legitimate offer.

sections.title: What to check before responding
sections.html:
First, find out how the sender got your name and address, most legitimate buyers pull that from county deed records, which is normal and not itself a red flag. Second, ask what they're basing the number on, your actual decimal interest, recent production, or a flat estimate applied to everyone in the mailing. If they can't or won't explain the basis for the number, that tells you something. Third, check whether there's a real Montana business address or registered agent behind the letter, beyond a bare PO box.

It's also worth pulling your own division order or recent royalty statements if you have them, and comparing the offer against what you're actually being paid. A number that ignores your real production history, or seems disconnected from what your check stubs show, is worth questioning before you sign anything back.

sections.title: Why urgency in the letter is the biggest tell
sections.html:
Language pushing you to respond within a short window, or implying the offer expires imminently, is one of the more reliable signs of a lowball approach. Mineral values don't typically shift so fast that a real offer needs to expire in a week. If a buyer is confident in their number, giving you time to verify it and even get a second opinion shouldn't threaten the deal.

We'd rather you take that time, even if it means comparing against our own quote, than sign something under pressure you haven't had a chance to check.

sections.title: Getting a second, verified number
sections.html:
Sending us the same documentation, your division order, recent statements, or the deed identifying the interest, gets you a comparison number built from your actual production and county activity rather than a mailing-list formula. If the original offer holds up against that comparison, that's useful information too. If it doesn't, you'll know before you've signed anything.

This doesn't cost you anything and doesn't obligate you to sell to anyone. It just gives you a second data point before making a decision that's hard to undo once a deed is recorded.

sections.title: If you already signed something
sections.html: If you've already signed and mailed back an unsolicited offer, check the closing timeline before assuming it's final, some transactions include a short window before funds transfer or the deed records where questions can still be raised, though this varies and isn't guaranteed. If you're unsure where things stand, an attorney can review the specific document faster than guessing on your own.

sections.title: What a legitimate buyer does differently
sections.html: A buyer working in good faith will typically tell you the operator and well their offer is based on, explain roughly how they arrived at the number, and give you a reasonable window to review the paperwork before signing. They will also answer follow-up questions directly rather than deflecting or repeating the same figure. None of that costs them anything if the offer is genuinely fair, which is exactly why its absence is worth noticing.

faqs.q: How did this company get your name and address for your Montana minerals?
faqs.a: Almost always from county deed or division order records, which are public. That alone isn't a sign of anything shady, most legitimate buyers work the same way.

faqs.q: Is it normal for the offer letter to have a deadline?
faqs.a: It's common but worth treating skeptically. A short deadline pressuring quick action is one of the more reliable signs a number may be lower than what your interest could actually get with time to compare.

faqs.q: Can you get a comparison quote without committing to anything?
faqs.a: Yes. Sending your documentation for a review doesn't obligate you to sell, it just gives you a second, documented number to weigh against whatever mailer offer you received.

faqs.q: You already signed and sent back an offer. Can you undo it?
faqs.a: It depends on where the transaction stands and the specific terms of what you signed. Check whether funds have transferred or the deed has been recorded, and if you're unsure, an attorney can review the document and tell you your options quickly.

items.name: Out-of-State Owners
items.meta: Live outside Montana but own minerals here? A retired operator explains how absentee owners verify a real offer, handle title work remotely, and close without a trip.

sections.html:
You don't have to fly to Montana to sell what you own here, but you do have to know what you're signing before you sign it from three states away.

A large share of Montana mineral owners we talk to don't live anywhere near the acreage. Families moved for work generations ago, kids inherited a piece of the old homestead and settled in Seattle or Minneapolis or Texas, and the minerals just stayed on the books in Montana while the people scattered. That distance makes the whole process feel murkier than it needs to be, no way to drive out and look at the well, no local contact to call, just paperwork arriving from a state you may not have visited in years.

The mechanics of selling don't actually require being local. Everything runs through documentation, title work, and a closing that can happen entirely by mail or overnight courier. What matters more for an out-of-state owner is knowing how to tell a legitimate offer from a lowball mailer, and understanding what to verify before signing anything.

sections.title: Why absentee owners get worse offers, and how to avoid it
sections.html:
Buyers who blanket-mail out-of-state owners often bank on the fact that someone three time zones away can't easily verify local activity, drive by the well, or call a neighbor to check the story. That gap gets exploited with mailers quoting flat, unverified numbers, sometimes well below what the interest would fetch from a buyer actually checking current royalty statements and nearby drilling activity. Distance from the property is not a reason to accept a worse number, it just means you need to lean harder on documentation instead of local knowledge.

The fix is straightforward: ask for the same documentation you'd want if you lived next door. What operator, what well, what's the recent production history, what's happening on adjacent acreage. A legitimate buyer answers those questions directly instead of just pushing you toward signing.

sections.title: Handling title and closing remotely
sections.html:
Mineral deeds get recorded at the county clerk and recorder's office where the minerals sit, and that recording doesn't require your physical presence in Montana. Closing documents are typically notarized wherever you happen to live, most banks, UPS stores, and shipping centers offer notary service, and then mailed back for recording. We've closed deals with owners who've genuinely never set foot in the state their minerals are in, and the process works the same as it would for a local seller.

The one thing that does slow down remote closings is incomplete or unclear title, an old deed with a maiden name that doesn't match current ID, an estate that was never formally probated, records split across a name change. None of that is unique to being out of state, but it's worth flagging early since it can add a few weeks to the title work regardless of where you live.

sections.title: Verifying who you're dealing with from a distance
sections.html:
Before signing anything, ask for a Montana business address or registered agent, ask how the buyer arrived at their number, and don't be afraid to ask for the offer in writing with time to have someone review it, an attorney, a family member who's local, whoever you trust. A legitimate buyer won't pressure you to sign same-day over the phone. If someone's pushing urgency, that's the biggest red flag regardless of how far away you live from the acreage.

It's also worth checking whether other family members received similar mailers, sometimes an entire heir group scattered across the country gets the same offer, and comparing notes among relatives can tell you a lot about whether a number is fair.

sections.title: Starting the process from out of state
sections.html: Send whatever documentation you have by mail, email, or scan, division order, old deed, probate paperwork, doesn't matter the format. We'll walk you through what your minerals are actually worth based on real activity in that county, not a mailer formula, and handle the closing paperwork so it works whether you're in Billings or three thousand miles away.

faqs.q: Do you need to travel to Montana to sell your minerals?
faqs.a: No. Deeds are recorded at the county level and documents are typically notarized wherever you live, then mailed for recording. Owners routinely close a sale without ever visiting the state.

faqs.q: How do you know an out-of-state offer isn't a scam?
faqs.a: Ask for specifics: the operator name, well information, and how the buyer arrived at their number. A legitimate buyer answers directly and doesn't pressure you to sign quickly. Verifying against a division order or courthouse record is always a reasonable ask.

faqs.q: Your grandmother's deed has her maiden name and you've never updated anything. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It can slow down title work, but it's a routine fix, usually a probate document or affidavit connecting the names. It's more common than you'd think and doesn't kill a deal, it just adds some time.

faqs.q: Can you split the sale process among siblings who live in different states?
faqs.a: Yes. Each heir can typically handle their own documentation and closing independently, even from different states, as long as everyone's decimal interest is clearly established.

items.name: Minerals in Probate & Estates
items.meta: Executor handling Montana mineral rights in an estate? A retired operator explains the probate sequence, valuation for the estate, and selling to multiple heirs cleanly.

sections.html:
An executor's job with mineral rights isn't to guess at a number, it's to get one that holds up when the whole estate gets settled.

If you're serving as executor or personal representative for a Montana estate that includes mineral rights, you're probably dealing with an asset none of the other estate property prepared you for. A house has comparable sales. A brokerage account has a statement balance. Mineral rights have neither, unless there's a current division order and royalty history, and even then the fair value for estate purposes takes some work to establish.

The good news is the process is well-trodden. Estates with oil and gas interests go through Montana probate courts regularly, especially in the eastern and central counties where mineral ownership is common, and there's a standard sequence for identifying, valuing, and eventually distributing or selling those interests.

sections.title: Identifying what the estate actually owns
sections.html:
Start with the deceased's records, deeds, division orders, old lease agreements, tax statements referencing oil and gas income. If those aren't complete, the county clerk and recorder's office in the county where the minerals sit can help trace ownership by name search. It's not unusual to find that an estate includes minerals nobody in the family fully remembered, especially if they've been non-producing for years or the deceased inherited them decades ago from their own parents.

Once identified, each interest needs its legal description, county, township, section, confirmed, along with whatever production or lease status currently applies. This becomes the basis for both the estate inventory and any eventual sale.

sections.title: Valuing minerals for the estate inventory
sections.html:
Montana probate typically requires a fair value for estate assets as of the date of death, which for mineral interests means pricing based on production history, lease status, and nearby activity at that point in time, not necessarily today. This is one area where getting an actual documented offer, even if the estate ultimately doesn't sell, gives the executor a defensible number for the inventory rather than a rough guess.

If the interest is producing, recent royalty statements around the date of death are the strongest evidence. If it's non-producing, the valuation leans more on lease status and drilling activity in the surrounding area at that time, the same factors we'd use to quote any non-producing tract.

sections.title: Selling through the estate versus distributing to heirs
sections.html:
Depending on the will's instructions and what the heirs want, minerals can either be sold by the estate itself with proceeds distributed among beneficiaries, or the interest can be distributed in kind to heirs who then decide individually whether to keep or sell. Selling through the estate is often simpler when there are multiple heirs who'd rather not become co-owners of a fractional mineral interest together, since it resolves the asset into cash before distribution rather than after.

If the will specifically directs the minerals to one heir, or if that heir wants to keep the family land connection, distribution in kind followed by an individual decision later makes more sense. Either path is common, and which one applies usually comes down to what's cleanest for that particular estate.

sections.title: Working with an executor on a review
sections.html: Send whatever estate documentation identifies the minerals, along with any division orders or lease paperwork available. We'll give you a documented, honest valuation you can use for the estate inventory, and if the estate decides to sell, we can walk through that process directly with you as executor, coordinated with whatever your probate attorney needs for the filing.

faqs.q: Do you need court approval to sell mineral rights out of an estate?
faqs.a: It depends on the specific probate proceeding and what authority the will or the court has granted the personal representative. In many straightforward Montana probates the executor can sell estate property without a separate court order, but your probate attorney can confirm what applies to this specific estate.

faqs.q: What if you can't find a division order or any record of the minerals producing?
faqs.a: That's common with older or dormant interests. We can still establish the legal description from deed or tax records and value the interest based on nearby activity, even without a production history.

faqs.q: Can you get a valuation before the estate is fully through probate?
faqs.a: Yes, a documented offer can be requested at any point in the process and used as supporting evidence for the estate inventory, whether or not the sale happens before probate closes.

faqs.q: Multiple heirs are set to inherit the same mineral interest. Should the estate sell it first?
faqs.a: Many executors find it simpler to sell through the estate and distribute cash proceeds, avoiding multiple heirs becoming co-owners of a small fractional interest. But if an heir wants to keep the family minerals, distributing in kind is equally valid.

faqs.q: What if the estate includes minerals in more than one Montana county?
faqs.a: Each county has its own clerk and recorder, so title work and any recorded deed of distribution typically need to be handled separately for each legal description. It adds some coordination but is not unusual for larger family estates with land accumulated over multiple generations.

image.alt: Minerals in Probate & Estates mineral rights

items.name: Fractional & Small Interests
items.meta: Own a tiny undivided percentage of Montana minerals split among heirs? A retired operator explains why fractional interests are worth selling and how the math works.

sections.html:
A one-sixty-fourth interest sounds too small to matter until you realize it's still yours, and it still pays, or could.

Montana mineral ownership has a way of fracturing over generations. A section that one family owned outright in 1920 might now be split among a dozen grandchildren and great-grandchildren, each holding a decimal interest so small it looks like a rounding error on the division order. We see this constantly, especially on older homestead sections across the eastern and central part of the state where minerals were reserved at patent and never consolidated.

The instinct a lot of small-interest owners have is that it's not worth the trouble, too small to sell, too small to bother tracking. That's usually wrong. Small doesn't mean worthless, it just means the math has to be done correctly, and a lot of buyers won't bother quoting tiny interests accurately because it's more work per dollar for them. That's exactly where a straightforward review helps.

sections.title: How a fractional interest actually gets valued
sections.html:
The starting point is always your decimal interest as it appears on the division order or, if you've never received one, as it can be traced through the deed and probate chain. From there, value comes down to the same basic factors as any mineral interest: is the underlying tract producing, what's the well's decline profile, and is there any drilling or leasing activity nearby. A one-thirty-second interest under an actively producing well in a good section can be worth more than a whole undivided interest in a dry, undrilled quarter section elsewhere.

Where fractional owners get shortchanged is when a buyer quotes off the surface acreage instead of the net mineral acres actually owned. If a section has 640 gross acres and your family's original patent covered 160 of them, and you're one of eight living heirs, your true net mineral acreage is a small fraction of what people assume from the county name alone. Getting that math right, from gross acres down to your actual decimal, is the first thing we do before quoting anyone.

sections.title: Why so many Montana interests ended up this fractured
sections.html:
Homestead-era patents in Montana often reserved or included mineral rights that passed down through wills, and rural families rarely did formal mineral deeds when dividing an estate, they just let the interest pass by inheritance to however many children or grandchildren existed at the time. Multiply that by two or three generations and you get interests measured in the hundredths or thousandths of a percent, owned by heirs scattered across the country who may not even know each other.

This is common enough in Montana oil and gas counties that operators and title companies deal with it routinely. It's not a sign anything went wrong with your family's paperwork, it's just how mineral ownership naturally dilutes without active consolidation.

sections.title: Consolidating versus selling piecemeal
sections.html:
Some heir groups choose to sell together as a family, combining several small interests into one transaction, which can simplify the paperwork and sometimes gets a slightly better combined number since the buyer is picking up more net mineral acres in one deal. Others sell individually on their own timeline, which works fine too, it just means each heir handles their own title documentation separately.

Neither approach is wrong. If your siblings or cousins also inherited a share of the same original tract, it's worth a conversation before anyone sells, mainly so everyone understands what the others are doing and nobody's surprised by a new co-owner showing up on the division order.

sections.title: Getting a small interest reviewed properly
sections.html: Send whatever you have, even if it's an old division order with someone else's name on it or a probate document from a parent's estate. Tracing a fractional interest through inheritance takes a bit more legwork than a straightforward deed, but it's routine work, and we'd rather spend the time getting your actual decimal right than hand you a lowball guess based on a rough estimate.

faqs.q: Is your interest too small to be worth selling?
faqs.a: Almost never. Small decimal interests still carry real value if the underlying well is producing, and buyers who work this space regularly are used to quoting fractional interests down to very small percentages.

faqs.q: You don't have a division order, only an old deed with your grandfather's name on it. Can you still figure out your interest?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Tracing ownership through a probate or inheritance chain from an original deed is common work, it just takes a bit more research than a current division order does.

faqs.q: Should you sell with your siblings together or separately?
faqs.a: Either works. Selling together as a group can simplify paperwork and sometimes yields a modest combined advantage, but selling individually on your own timeline is equally valid if that's what works for your family.

faqs.q: How small of an interest will actually get a real offer?
faqs.a: There's no fixed cutoff. What matters more than the size of the percentage is whether there's production or lease activity to value it against. Send the documentation you have and we'll tell you honestly what's realistic.

items.name: Leased but Undrilled
items.meta: Signed a Montana oil and gas lease, cashed the bonus check, but no well ever came? A retired operator explains what leased-undrilled minerals are worth and why timing matters.

sections.html:
You signed the lease, cashed the bonus, and then nothing happened. That's more common in this business than people expect, and it doesn't mean the acreage is worthless.

A lot of Montana mineral owners have been through exactly this: a landman shows up, or a letter arrives, offering a lease bonus per acre and a royalty fraction if a well is ever drilled. You sign, the check clears, and then months or years pass with no rig, no permit, sometimes not even a phone call. Leases in Montana typically run a primary term of three to five years, and plenty of them expire with nothing drilled at all, especially on flank or lower-priority acreage.

That doesn't make the interest worthless, but it does change how it gets valued compared to a producing well. A leased-and-undrilled interest is essentially a bet on future activity, and pricing it honestly means being straight about how likely that activity actually is given what's happening on the acreage around you.

sections.title: What a lease actually signals, and what it doesn't
sections.html:
An operator paying a lease bonus is making a calculated wager that the acreage is worth holding for a few years while they evaluate it alongside their broader drilling program. It does not guarantee a well gets drilled. Operators lease far more acreage than they ultimately develop, holding it as inventory or optionality, and a lot of leased Montana ground simply expires undrilled when capital gets allocated elsewhere in a given year.

What matters more than the fact of the lease itself is what's happening around your acreage. Are neighboring sections seeing permits filed or rigs move in. Is the operator who leased you actively drilling elsewhere in the county right now, or have they gone quiet basin-wide. Those signals tell you more about your real odds of a well than the lease document does.

sections.title: Why buyers price this differently than producing interests
sections.html:
A producing well gives a buyer real numbers, actual royalty checks, a visible decline curve, something concrete to price against. A leased-but-undrilled interest is priced more against probability and nearby activity, which naturally makes offers more conservative than what you'd see on an established producer. That's not a buyer lowballing you, it's the honest math of paying for something that might never generate income versus something that already is.

That said, the size of the lease bonus itself and the specific operator involved both carry information. A bonus well above what's typical for the area, or a lease from an operator with an active rig program elsewhere in the basin, both suggest higher real odds of eventual drilling than a bare-minimum bonus from a company that hasn't drilled a well in Montana in years.

sections.title: The clock on your lease matters
sections.html:
Check your lease's primary term and any extension or option clauses. As that term runs down without a well, the lease either expires, freeing your minerals to be released to someone else or left open, or the operator exercises an option to extend it, sometimes with an additional bonus payment. Knowing where you are in that timeline matters if you're weighing a sale now versus waiting to see whether the lease gets extended or a permit gets filed before it expires.

Some owners choose to sell while leased, transferring the bonus history and lease terms to the buyer along with the mineral interest. Others wait to see whether a well actually gets drilled before deciding, since a producing well is a much easier thing to value. Both are reasonable, depending on how much uncertainty you're comfortable holding.

sections.title: Getting a leased-undrilled interest looked at
sections.html: Send your lease agreement along with any correspondence from the operator. We'll look at what's leasing and permitting nearby, check the operator's recent activity in the basin, and give you an honest read on where your acreage likely sits in their plans, along with what that means for a fair offer today versus waiting.

faqs.q: Your lease is about to expire with no well drilled. Should you sell now or wait?
faqs.a: It depends on nearby activity. If neighboring sections are seeing permits or drilling, waiting for a possible extension or new lease could pay off. If the operator has gone quiet basin-wide, selling now for a known amount may make more sense than waiting on uncertain future activity.

faqs.q: Does a bigger lease bonus mean a well is more likely to get drilled?
faqs.a: It's a signal, not a guarantee. A higher-than-typical bonus can suggest the operator sees strong potential, but plenty of well-leased acreage still goes undrilled when a company's capital plan shifts. Recent nearby permits are usually a stronger indicator than bonus size alone.

faqs.q: Can you sell your minerals if they're currently under an active lease?
faqs.a: Yes. The lease transfers with the mineral interest, and the buyer steps into your position as lessor, collecting any future bonus or royalty if the lease is extended or a well is drilled.

faqs.q: What happens to your minerals if the lease just expires with nothing drilled?
faqs.a: They're released and you're free to lease again, sell, or hold. Nothing about ownership changes, you simply go back to being unleased acreage until another operator, or the same one, decides to lease it again.

image.alt: Leased but Undrilled mineral rights

items.name: Non-Producing Minerals
items.meta: No wells, no royalty checks, expired lease. Non-producing Montana minerals still have value. A retired operator explains how they're priced and when to consider a sale.

sections.html:
No well, no royalty check, no lease on file. It's easy to assume that means no value. It usually doesn't mean that.

Non-producing is the category we probably field the most questions about, because it's the hardest for an owner to make sense of on their own. There's no division order to point to, no monthly check as a reference point, sometimes not even a lease history. Just a legal description in a county and a family story that somebody, sometime, owned minerals there.

Montana has a lot of acreage like this, sections that were leased once decades ago and never drilled, ground in counties without much current activity, minerals that simply sat quiet through multiple owner generations. None of that means the interest is worth nothing. It means the value comes from a different set of questions than a producing well does.

sections.title: How non-producing minerals actually get valued
sections.html:
Without a royalty history, value comes from three things: what's happening on the acreage around you, what play or formation underlies your section, and how likely it is an operator leases or drills there in a reasonable timeframe. A non-producing tract in Richland County near active Bakken development gets valued very differently than a non-producing tract in a county with no oil and gas activity in a decade. Same legal status, very different number.

This is where knowing the basins matters. If your minerals sit on the western edge of the Williston, near Elm Coulee, or in a part of the Powder River Basin where CBM activity has cycled through before, there's a real basis for pricing even without current production. If they're in a county with essentially no drilling history, the honest answer is that the value is mostly speculative, and we'll tell you that directly rather than inflate a quote.

sections.title: Why some owners still choose to sell non-producing minerals
sections.html:
Selling a non-producing interest converts an asset with uncertain, possibly distant future value into cash today. For owners who don't want to keep tracking an interest that may never pay, who inherited it as part of a larger estate, or who'd simply rather have a known amount than an open-ended maybe, that trade makes sense. It's essentially selling the optionality, the chance that drilling eventually happens, to a buyer willing to hold that patience.

Other owners prefer to hold non-producing minerals indefinitely, treating them as a long-shot asset with no carrying cost beyond occasionally checking county records. That's a reasonable choice too, particularly if there's no urgent need for the cash and some sentimental or generational reason to keep the family's original mineral ownership intact.

sections.title: What buyers actually check before quoting
sections.html:
Recent permit filings and rig activity in your township, whether any adjacent sections have been leased recently and at what bonus, what formation or play the section sits over, and whether there's any operator with stated plans in that part of the county. All of that is public record through the Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation and county courthouse filings, and it's exactly what we look at before putting a number on non-producing acreage rather than guessing off the county name alone.

We'd rather spend the time checking that activity than send a generic lowball offer, because non-producing doesn't mean uniform, some non-producing sections are genuinely close to seeing a well, and some genuinely aren't.

sections.title: Getting a non-producing interest reviewed
sections.html: Send whatever documentation identifies the legal description, county, township, and section, even an old deed or tax statement is enough to start. We'll check current activity in that area and give you an honest read on what, if anything, it's realistically worth today.

faqs.q: If there's no well and no lease, is there really any value at all?
faqs.a: Sometimes yes, sometimes it's genuinely minimal. It depends on activity nearby and what formation underlies the section. Active basins with recent leasing or permitting nearby support real value even without your own production; quiet counties with no recent history often don't.

faqs.q: Your family's minerals were leased once decades ago but never drilled. Does that old lease still matter?
faqs.a: Not directly, since leases typically expire after their primary term without drilling. But historical leasing activity can be a useful signal that operators have had past interest in the area, which is worth mentioning when getting a review.

faqs.q: Should you try to get your minerals leased before selling?
faqs.a: It depends on whether there's realistic near-term interest from an operator. If nothing's actively leasing nearby, waiting on a lease that may not come could tie up the decision for years. A direct sale skips that uncertainty.

faqs.q: How do you even find out what county and section your family's minerals are in?
faqs.a: Old deeds, tax statements, or probate records usually carry the legal description. If you're unsure, the county clerk and recorder's office where you believe the land was located can typically help trace it from a name search.

faqs.q: Does the Montana Board of Oil and Gas Conservation track your specific interest?
faqs.a: The board tracks wells, permits, and spacing units by legal description, not individual mineral owners directly. Once we have your township and section, we can check that public record for any recent permitting or drilling activity nearby that would bear on value.

items.name: Trust-Owned Minerals
items.meta: Trustee managing Montana mineral rights inside a family trust? A retired operator explains fiduciary valuation duties, beneficiary considerations, and how a trust sale works.

sections.html:
A trustee's obligation with mineral rights goes beyond deciding to sell or hold, it means documenting why that choice serves the beneficiaries, and that starts with a real number.

Montana families put a lot of things into trusts, ranches, mineral rights, sometimes both together as a single package meant to stay in the family. If you're serving as trustee for one of these and the trust holds oil and gas minerals, you're managing an asset that doesn't behave like the trust's other holdings. It doesn't have a daily price. It may or may not be producing. And unlike a stock or bond, there's no simple statement to hand beneficiaries showing what it's currently worth.

As trustee, you have a fiduciary duty to manage trust assets prudently, which for minerals usually means understanding what's actually owned, whether it's producing income consistent with the trust's purpose, and whether holding or selling better serves the beneficiaries given the trust's terms and their needs.

sections.title: What prudent management of trust minerals looks like
sections.html:
The starting point is the same as any trust asset: know what you have. Pull the division order if the trust has one, confirm the legal description and county, and establish whether the interest is currently producing, leased-but-undrilled, or dormant. From there, a documented valuation, ideally more than one data point, whether that's a formal appraisal, a documented cash offer, or both, gives you something defensible to reference if beneficiaries ever question the decision.

This matters more with mineral interests than most trust assets because the value swings meaningfully with commodity prices and drilling activity, sometimes within a single year. A number that looked fair eighteen months ago may not reflect current conditions, which is worth checking periodically even if the trust isn't actively considering a sale.

sections.title: When holding makes sense versus when selling does
sections.html:
If the trust's purpose includes generating income for beneficiaries and the minerals are producing steadily, holding them can align well with that mandate, functioning similarly to any income-producing trust asset. If the trust document calls for eventual distribution of principal to beneficiaries, or if the minerals are non-producing and unlikely to generate near-term income, converting them to cash may better serve the trust's actual purpose than holding an illiquid, hard-to-value asset indefinitely.

Some trusts specifically instruct the trustee to keep mineral interests in the family; others are silent and leave it to the trustee's judgment. Either way, documenting the reasoning, and the valuation behind it, protects you as trustee regardless of which direction you choose.

sections.title: Multiple beneficiaries and competing preferences
sections.html:
It's common for beneficiaries to disagree, one wants to keep the family minerals for sentimental reasons, another wants their share converted to cash sooner. As trustee, your obligation runs to the trust's terms and the interests of all beneficiaries collectively, not to any one beneficiary's preference. A clear, documented valuation helps here too, since it gives everyone the same real number to react to instead of competing guesses about what the minerals might be worth.

If the trust allows partial distribution or division of the interest among beneficiaries who want different outcomes, that's sometimes a workable middle path, though it does mean more paperwork and eventually multiple smaller interests rather than one trust holding.

sections.title: Working with a trustee on a mineral review
sections.html: Send the trust's division order or the deed identifying the mineral interest, along with the county and legal description. We'll give you a documented valuation you can use for trust accounting or a beneficiary discussion, and if the trust decides to sell, we can walk through the process directly with you and whatever attorney or accountant the trust works with.

faqs.q: Do you need a formal appraisal, or is a documented cash offer enough for trust records?
faqs.a: It depends on your state's trust accounting requirements and what the trust document specifies, but a documented cash offer tied to actual royalty or lease data is often accepted as reasonable supporting evidence, sometimes alongside a formal appraisal. Your trust attorney or accountant can confirm what's required for this specific trust.

faqs.q: Can you sell only part of the trust's mineral interest instead of all of it?
faqs.a: Yes, if the trust document allows it. Partial sales are common when a trustee wants to generate some liquidity while keeping a portion of the interest for continued income or family connection.

faqs.q: What if beneficiaries disagree about whether to sell?
faqs.a: Your duty as trustee is to the trust's terms and the collective interest of all beneficiaries, not any single preference. A documented, defensible valuation helps ground that decision in facts rather than competing opinions.

faqs.q: How often should trust-owned minerals be reevaluated?
faqs.a: There's no fixed rule, but checking in periodically, especially after any major activity nearby or a commodity price shift, keeps the trust's records current and helps you respond quickly if a sale or lease decision needs to be made.

faqs.q: Can a successor trustee pick up where a prior trustee left off on valuing trust minerals?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is common. A successor trustee inherits the same fiduciary duty and can request an updated valuation at any point, especially if the prior review is more than a year or two old or commodity conditions have shifted since.
