items.name: Selling for Liquidity
items.meta: Medical bills, retirement income, or debt pressure? A retired operator explains how selling Montana mineral rights converts royalty uncertainty into cash on your timeline.

sections.html:
There's a difference between minerals that are convenient to own and minerals you actually need cash from right now, and it's worth being honest about which one you're facing.

Most of the owners we talk to who are selling under real pressure aren't doing it because they've stopped caring about the family's mineral history. They're doing it because a medical bill came due, retirement income needs to stretch further than a small unpredictable royalty check allows, or debt needs paying down faster than a monthly statement can cover. Those are practical decisions, and there's no reason to feel like selling under those circumstances is a lesser choice than holding for sentiment.

What we'd rather you avoid is making that decision with a lowball number because the pressure made you skip comparing offers. Urgency and getting a fair price aren't actually in conflict, a straightforward review can move fast without cutting your number.

sections.title: Why royalty income doesn't fix a cash-now problem
sections.html:
Royalty checks, even from a producing well, are inherently unpredictable month to month. Prices swing, wells decline, operators sometimes hold payments for months while resolving title issues on other owners in the same well. If you're facing a bill due in thirty days or a fixed retirement budget that needs certainty, waiting on royalty income to accumulate rarely solves the problem the way a lump sum does. That's the core tradeoff: keep the asset and its long-run, uncertain income, or convert it to a known number today.

This isn't an argument that selling is always right, plenty of owners are fine riding out royalty volatility because they don't need the cash on a specific timeline. It's specifically for the situation where the timeline itself is the pressure.

sections.title: How fast a sale can actually move
sections.html:
Once title is clear and documentation, a division order or deed, is in hand, a straightforward mineral sale in Montana can close in a matter of weeks rather than months. The slowest parts are usually title work, confirming the chain of ownership is clean, and any probate steps if the interest passed through an estate that wasn't fully settled. If your paperwork is in order, the process moves considerably faster than most real estate transactions.

If time truly matters, say so up front. We can prioritize title review and get you a documented offer quickly, and you can weigh that against whatever timeline you're actually working against, medical, financial, or otherwise.

sections.title: Getting a fair number even under pressure
sections.html:
The honest way to avoid a lowball offer when you're in a hurry is the same as when you're not: ask how the number was reached, request it against your actual royalty statements or lease documentation, and don't be pressured into signing same-day without at least reading through the terms. A buyer who understands your timeline should still be willing to show their work.

If you have time to get even one comparison quote, that's worth doing. If the pressure is severe enough that speed matters more than shopping around, focus on documentation instead, make sure whoever you're selling to can show exactly how they landed on the number, tied to your production history or nearby activity, rather than a flat unexplained figure.

sections.title: Starting when time matters
sections.html: Send your division order or deed and let us know your timeline. We'll move as fast as the title work allows and give you a number grounded in your actual production or lease history, not a rushed guess, so you're not trading speed for a fair price.

faqs.q: How fast can a mineral sale actually close if you need the cash soon?
faqs.a: With clean title and a division order or deed in hand, a few weeks is realistic. The main variable is whether title work uncovers anything, like an unresolved estate, that needs to be cleared first.

faqs.q: Will you get a lower offer if you tell the buyer you need the money quickly?
faqs.a: It shouldn't work that way with a legitimate buyer, the offer should be based on your production or lease documentation regardless of your timeline. If a buyer drops their number specifically because you disclosed urgency, that's worth pushing back on.

faqs.q: Is selling minerals for liquidity better than borrowing against them?
faqs.a: It depends on your situation. Selling gives you a lump sum with no ongoing obligation; borrowing keeps the asset but adds debt and interest. This isn't financial advice, it's worth discussing with a financial advisor if you're weighing the two.

faqs.q: What if your minerals are tied up in an estate that hasn't been settled?
faqs.a: That can add time to the title work, but it doesn't prevent a sale, it just means the probate step typically needs to happen first, or in parallel. We can tell you what's needed once we see your documentation.

faqs.q: Will selling your minerals affect your taxes or retirement benefits?
faqs.a: A sale is typically a capital transaction with its own tax treatment, separate from ordinary royalty income, and it can interact with other financial planning depending on your situation. That is a question for your accountant or financial advisor, not something to guess at on your own.

items.name: Mineral Rights in Divorce
items.meta: Splitting mineral rights in a Montana divorce is harder than dividing a bank account. A former operator explains valuation, buyouts, and selling as a clean settlement option.

sections.html:
A bank account splits in half cleanly. Mineral rights don't, and that's usually the whole problem.

We've talked to a fair number of Montana couples working through a divorce where minerals showed up on the marital property list almost as an afterthought, then became the hardest line item to settle. Unlike a house or a retirement account, mineral rights don't have an easy market price. There's no listing service, no comparable sales database most attorneys can pull from, and the value swings with commodity prices, decline curves, and whether the acreage is producing at all. That uncertainty is exactly what stalls a settlement.

There are really three ways this usually resolves: one spouse keeps the interest and buys the other out, the interest gets divided into two smaller fractional pieces that each spouse holds separately going forward, or both spouses sell and split the cash. Each has real tradeoffs, and which one makes sense depends a lot on whether either of you actually wants to remain a mineral owner after the paperwork is signed.

sections.title: Why an appraisal alone doesn't settle it
sections.html:
Attorneys sometimes order a reserve report or a formal valuation to put a number on mineral rights for the marital estate. That's useful for the court filing, but a reserve report values future production under assumptions about price and decline that a cash buyer may see differently, and it costs money and weeks to produce. In our experience, getting an actual cash offer alongside any formal appraisal gives both spouses a real, checkable number rather than a theoretical one, and it often moves the settlement forward faster than waiting on paperwork.

If the interest is small, a few net mineral acres inherited from one spouse's family, the cost of a formal appraisal can eat up a meaningful share of the value itself. In those cases a straightforward buyer quote, backed by the division order and recent royalty history, is usually the more practical path.

sections.title: Splitting the interest versus one spouse keeping it
sections.html:
Dividing the mineral interest itself, so each spouse ends up owning half the decimal interest going forward, is legally simple but practically messy. It means two separate owners each getting their own division order, their own smaller royalty checks, and dealing with the same operator independently for years after the divorce is final. Most people who go this route don't love staying financially connected to an ex through a shared production well, even indirectly.

A cleaner option is often a buyout: one spouse keeps the full interest and pays the other their share of its value in cash or against other marital assets. That requires agreeing on a number, which is where a real cash offer helps settle the negotiation instead of two competing guesses.

sections.title: Selling outright and splitting proceeds
sections.html:
If neither spouse particularly wants to remain a mineral owner, and this comes up more than people expect, selling the whole interest and splitting the proceeds through the settlement is often the simplest resolution. It converts an illiquid, hard-to-value asset into a fixed number both attorneys can work with, and it avoids either party having to track royalty statements from an ex-spouse's family land for the next decade.

This route works particularly well when the minerals sit under acreage that's not directly tied to family land either spouse feels emotionally attached to keeping.

sections.title: Where the process starts
sections.html: Whichever direction makes sense for your settlement, it starts the same way: pull the division order and recent royalty statements so there's a documented, current picture of what's owned and what it's producing. We're happy to give both spouses and their attorneys an honest number to work from, whether that leads to a buyout, a sale, or just a clearer basis for negotiation.

faqs.q: Does mineral value in a divorce depend only on whether the well is currently producing?
faqs.a: Current production is the biggest factor, but not the only one. A non-producing interest with an active lease and nearby drilling can still carry real value based on what the lease bonus and offset activity suggest, even without a royalty check history yet.

faqs.q: Can you get a real offer before the divorce is finalized?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash offer can be requested at any point and doesn't obligate either spouse to sell. Many attorneys use a documented offer as a settlement reference point even if the sale itself happens later or not at all.

faqs.q: What if the minerals were inherited by only one spouse?
faqs.a: Whether inherited minerals count as separate or marital property depends on Montana law and the specifics of the marriage, including whether the interest was commingled with marital assets. That's a question for your attorney, but valuing the interest itself works the same regardless of which side of that line it falls on.

faqs.q: Is it faster to split the decimal interest than to sell or buy out?
faqs.a: It's faster on paper but often creates more long-term hassle, since both spouses end up as separate owners dealing with the operator independently for years. A buyout or outright sale usually resolves things more completely.

interest-types.title: Mineral Interest Types

items.name: Mineral Rights
items.meta: Understand what owning Montana mineral rights actually means, from split estate to royalty mechanics, explained by a retired E&P engineer before you sell or lease.

sections.html:
Owning minerals in Montana rarely means owning the ground itself, and that distinction confuses more sellers than anything else we explain.

Mineral rights are the legal right to whatever's beneath the surface, oil, gas, coal, and other subsurface resources, separate from ownership of the surface land itself. In Montana, especially on ground that was homesteaded or patented decades ago, it's extremely common for the mineral estate to have been split from the surface estate at some point, meaning you can own the minerals under a section of land you've never set foot on, while someone else entirely owns and farms the surface.

This split, called split estate, is the foundation for almost everything else about how Montana mineral ownership works: who gets contacted for a lease, who receives royalty checks if a well is drilled, and who has to be dealt with separately if there's ever a dispute over surface access for drilling equipment.

sections.title: The mineral estate as the dominant estate
sections.html:
Montana law, like most oil and gas states, treats the mineral estate as dominant over the surface estate, meaning the mineral owner or their lessee generally has the legal right to reasonable use of the surface to access and produce the minerals below, even if someone else owns that surface. In practice this gets negotiated through surface use agreements when a well is planned, but it's the legal backbone that makes drilling on split-estate land possible at all.

For a mineral owner, this matters mostly when a lease is being negotiated or a well gets permitted nearby, it's not something you have to actively manage day to day if you're just holding the interest. But it's useful to understand why a landman might show up asking about your minerals on land you don't otherwise have any connection to.

sections.title: What owning minerals actually entitles you to
sections.html:
Owning the full mineral estate gives you the right to lease the minerals to an operator in exchange for a bonus payment and a royalty share of future production, or to drill them yourself, though almost no individual mineral owners do that. It also gives you the right to negotiate lease terms, receive division order paperwork once a well is drilled, and collect royalty payments proportional to your ownership share within the well's spacing unit.

It does not automatically entitle you to surface access, farming rights, hunting rights, or anything above ground, those stay with whoever owns the surface unless you happen to own both. Owners sometimes assume mineral rights include some claim to the land itself; they don't, and that's worth being clear on before any conversation with a buyer or an operator.

sections.title: How Montana mineral ownership commonly gets fractured
sections.html:
A single original mineral estate, say the full interest under a 640-acre section, routinely fractures over generations through inheritance, ending up owned in small decimal percentages by a dozen or more heirs scattered across different states. That fracturing doesn't reduce the total value of the minerals, it just divides who's entitled to what share of any royalty or bonus payment. Your division order, once a well is drilled, will show your exact decimal interest based on however the original estate was divided down to you.

This is one reason Montana mineral transactions require careful title work, confirming exactly what percentage of the mineral estate a given owner actually holds, tracing back through however many inheritances or prior sales occurred.

sections.title: Understanding your own mineral interest before deciding anything
sections.html: Before leasing or selling, it helps to know exactly what you own: full mineral rights, a royalty-only interest, or something else, and what county and legal description it applies to. Send whatever deed or division order documentation you have and we can help clarify exactly what kind of interest you hold and what that means for a lease or sale conversation.

faqs.q: If you sell your mineral rights, do you lose your land too?
faqs.a: Only if you also own the surface and specifically include it in the sale. Most mineral transactions involve only the subsurface interest, the surface estate, if you own it, stays yours unless you separately agree to sell that too.

faqs.q: Can someone drill on your land without your permission if they own the minerals?
faqs.a: If the mineral estate is dominant and properly leased, the mineral owner or their lessee generally has a legal right to reasonable surface access, though this is typically worked out through a surface use agreement, and Montana has specific statutes governing that process.

faqs.q: What's the difference between owning mineral rights and owning a royalty interest?
faqs.a: Full mineral rights include the right to lease and negotiate terms with an operator. A royalty interest is a narrower right to a share of production income without the leasing authority. Knowing which one you hold changes how a transaction works.

faqs.q: How do you find out exactly what percentage of the minerals you own?
faqs.a: A division order from a producing well will state your exact decimal interest. If there's no well yet, your deed and any probate or inheritance documents establish your ownership share, which we can help trace if the paperwork is unclear.

items.name: Royalty Interests
items.meta: Own a royalty interest in a producing Montana well? A retired operator breaks down how royalty checks are calculated, what deductions mean, and how a sale is valued.

sections.html:
The royalty check tells you what you were paid last month. It doesn't tell you what the interest is actually worth if you decided to sell it.

A royalty interest is your right to a share of the value of oil or gas produced from a well, free of the costs of drilling and operating it, in exchange for having leased your minerals to the operator. It's the most common way Montana mineral owners actually experience oil and gas income, a monthly or periodic check calculated against your decimal interest and the lease's royalty fraction, typically somewhere in the range operators and mineral owners negotiated when the lease was signed.

Whether you hold the full mineral estate with a royalty flowing from your own lease, or a royalty carved out separately as an NPRI or ORRI, understanding how that check is actually calculated is the foundation for knowing whether a sale offer is fair.

sections.title: How your royalty check actually gets calculated
sections.html:
Start with the well's gross production and the price the operator realizes for the oil or gas sold. Multiply that by your decimal interest, your specific ownership fraction within the well's spacing unit, and then by the royalty rate specified in your lease. What often confuses owners is the deduction line, many leases allow the operator to deduct post-production costs, transportation, processing, gathering, before calculating your royalty, which means your net check is smaller than a simple gross calculation would suggest. Reading your own lease's deduction language matters here, since not all leases handle this the same way.

Your division order should show your exact decimal interest, and your monthly or quarterly royalty statement should itemize gross production, price received, deductions if any, and your net payment. If those numbers look inconsistent month to month, that's usually just normal production decline and price variation, not necessarily an error, though it's always worth checking if something looks clearly wrong.

sections.title: Why royalty value is more than last month's check times some multiple
sections.html:
A common mistake is assuming a royalty interest is worth a fixed multiple of the most recent check, times twelve, times some round number. Real valuation has to account for the well's decline curve, since production and therefore royalty income drops over time, often faster in the first few years than later. A buyer is really estimating the total remaining income stream over the well's productive life, discounted for the fact that money later is worth less than money now, rather than extrapolating last month's number indefinitely.

This is also why two royalty interests with identical current monthly checks can be worth different amounts, one might be on a well early in a long decline with years of production ahead, the other on a well nearing the end of its economic life. Knowing where your well sits on that curve, which we can usually estimate from a few months of statements, matters more than the current check size alone.

sections.title: Holding versus selling a royalty interest
sections.html:
Holding a royalty interest means continuing to receive income tied to the well's actual production, with all the volatility that involves, price swings, decline, occasional operator delays in payment, but with the potential upside if prices rise or the well outperforms expectations. Selling converts that uncertain future stream into a known amount today, trading potential upside for certainty. Neither is inherently better; it depends on whether you value the ongoing income or the lump sum more, given your own financial situation.

Some owners split the difference by selling a portion of their royalty interest and keeping the rest, which is worth asking about if you'd like some liquidity without giving up all future income.

sections.title: Getting your royalty interest reviewed
sections.html: Send your division order and a few recent royalty statements. That's enough for us to estimate where your well sits on its decline curve and give you an honest number for a full or partial sale, explained plainly rather than buried in jargon.

faqs.q: Why do post-production deductions reduce your royalty check?
faqs.a: Many leases allow the operator to deduct costs like gathering, transportation, and processing before calculating your royalty, depending on the specific lease language. It's normal, but worth understanding since it explains the gap between gross production value and your net check.

faqs.q: Can you sell just part of your royalty interest instead of all of it?
faqs.a: Yes, partial sales are common. You can sell a portion of your decimal interest or a set number of years of royalty income while retaining the rest, which lets you get some liquidity while keeping ongoing income.

faqs.q: Your royalty checks have been shrinking every month. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Wells naturally decline in production over time, often steeply in the first couple of years and then more gradually. Shrinking checks alone aren't necessarily a red flag, though it's worth reviewing your statements if the drop seems unusually sharp or sudden.

faqs.q: How many months of statements do you need to value your royalty interest?
faqs.a: Three to six months gives a reasonable read on the decline trend, though even one or two recent statements alongside the division order is enough to start a conversation.

items.name: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
items.meta: Own a non-participating royalty interest in Montana? A retired operator explains what NPRI means, how it differs from mineral rights, and how it's valued for sale.

sections.html:
You get a royalty check, but you never get a say in the lease. That's exactly what a non-participating royalty interest is, and it confuses a lot of owners the first time they see it on a deed.

A non-participating royalty interest, usually shortened to NPRI, is a carved-out right to a share of production income that does not carry any of the leasing rights that come with owning full mineral rights. You get paid your share of royalty if a well is drilled and produces, but you have no say in negotiating the lease terms, no right to bonus payments if the minerals get leased, and no vote if the mineral owner decides not to lease at all.

This shows up often in Montana on land where a prior owner sold or reserved the surface and full mineral rights but carved out a royalty percentage for themselves or a family member, sometimes going back to an original homestead transaction. If your deed uses language like 'reserving unto grantor a royalty interest' without mentioning leasing rights, that's almost certainly an NPRI rather than full mineral ownership.

sections.title: How NPRI differs from owning full minerals
sections.html:
The mineral owner, sometimes called the executive rights holder, controls whether and to whom the minerals get leased, negotiates the bonus payment and royalty fraction, and keeps any bonus money for themselves. As an NPRI holder, you're entitled only to your specified share of production royalty once a well is producing, calculated against your NPRI fraction, not the lease's full royalty rate necessarily, depending on how your interest was originally created.

This distinction matters a lot when a lease gets negotiated, since you have no input on the deal even though your income depends entirely on it. If the mineral owner negotiates a low royalty rate or delays leasing indefinitely, that directly affects what you receive, with no ability on your part to push back or negotiate separately.

sections.title: How NPRI gets valued for a sale
sections.html:
Valuing an NPRI works much like valuing a royalty interest generally: it comes down to your specific fraction, the well's current or likely production, and the lease terms governing the royalty rate. Because you don't control leasing, buyers also look at who does, is the executive rights holder actively leasing the property, or has it sat unleased for years with no clear path to development, since that affects how likely your NPRI is to ever generate income if it hasn't already.

If your NPRI is already tied to a producing well, valuation is fairly straightforward from your royalty statement history. If it's tied to unleased or undrilled acreage, the value depends more on whether the mineral owner has shown any recent interest in leasing, which is worth finding out if you can before getting a quote.

sections.title: Common ways NPRIs get created in Montana
sections.html:
Family land transactions historically created a lot of these, a parent selling land to a child but reserving a royalty for their own lifetime, or a seller retaining a royalty interest as part of a larger land sale decades ago while passing full mineral rights, including leasing control, to the buyer. Estate planning also creates NPRIs when a will splits an interest, giving one heir the executive rights and another heir just the royalty benefit.

If you inherited an NPRI without much explanation of how it came to be, the original deed language, findable at the county clerk's office, usually spells out exactly how the interest was reserved and its specific fraction.

sections.title: Getting an NPRI reviewed
sections.html: Send your deed or division order, whatever identifies your specific NPRI fraction and the well or lease it's tied to. We'll walk through what it's actually paying, or likely to pay if unleased, and give you an honest number if you're considering a sale.

faqs.q: Can you lease your own NPRI to an operator directly?
faqs.a: No. Leasing authority, called executive rights, belongs to whoever holds the full mineral estate, not the NPRI holder. You collect royalty once a lease is in place and production begins, but you don't negotiate or sign the lease yourself.

faqs.q: Your NPRI has never paid anything. Is it worth selling?
faqs.a: It depends on whether the underlying minerals are leased or likely to be leased. An NPRI tied to unleased acreage with no nearby activity carries more speculative value than one tied to acreage an operator is actively working.

faqs.q: How is your NPRI fraction different from the well's overall royalty rate?
faqs.a: Your NPRI fraction was set when the interest was originally created and applies against whatever royalty the mineral owner negotiates in the lease. The math can get specific depending on the exact deed language, which is worth reviewing carefully.

faqs.q: Why would someone create an NPRI instead of just keeping full mineral rights?
faqs.a: It's often used in family land sales or estate planning to give someone royalty income without handing over control of leasing decisions, letting the seller or one heir keep decision-making authority while sharing the financial benefit.

image.alt: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI) mineral rights

items.name: Surface vs. Mineral Estate
items.meta: Confused why you own minerals but not the land above them? A retired operator explains Montana split estate, surface use agreements, and how it affects a mineral sale.

sections.html:
You can own what's under a piece of Montana ground without owning an acre of the ground itself, and that single fact explains most of the confusion we hear from new sellers.

Split estate is the term for land where the surface and the minerals beneath it are owned separately, often by completely different people or families with no relationship to each other. It's extremely common across Montana, tracing back to how the federal government patented homestead land in the early twentieth century, sometimes reserving minerals to the government, sometimes granting minerals but not surface, or the reverse, and later through private sales where a family kept the minerals but sold the surface, or vice versa.

If you own minerals but not the surface above them, you may never have set foot on the land, and the person farming or ranching it may have no idea a well could someday be drilled there under their pasture. Both facts are normal, and understanding the split explains a lot about how leasing, drilling, and eventually selling your minerals actually works.

sections.title: How Montana land ended up split this way
sections.html:
A lot of eastern and central Montana was homesteaded under federal land laws that in some cases reserved subsurface mineral rights to the government while granting surface patents to settlers, particularly on land patented under certain acts in the early 1900s. In other cases, private landowners later sold the surface for ranching or farming while retaining the minerals for themselves or their heirs, sometimes explicitly to preserve future oil and gas potential, sometimes almost as an afterthought in the deed language.

Either way, the result is the same today: county records in oil and gas counties are full of tracts where the surface owner and mineral owner are unrelated parties, and that split has often persisted and further fractured through multiple generations of inheritance on each side independently.

sections.title: Why the mineral estate generally has surface access rights
sections.html:
Montana law treats the mineral estate as dominant, meaning the mineral owner, or more practically their oil and gas lessee once a lease is signed, generally has the right to reasonable use of the surface to explore for and produce the minerals, even without the surface owner's consent, though this is usually worked out through negotiated surface use agreements rather than forced entry. Montana has specific statutes governing notice and compensation to surface owners when drilling activity affects agricultural or grazing land.

For a mineral owner, this matters less in day-to-day terms and more if a well ever actually gets planned on your specific acreage, at which point the operator, not you personally, typically handles the surface use negotiation with whoever owns that ground.

sections.title: What split estate does and doesn't change about selling minerals
sections.html:
Selling your mineral interest doesn't require any involvement from the surface owner, and it doesn't grant the buyer any surface rights beyond the standard reasonable-access rights that come with mineral ownership generally. The transaction is between you and the mineral buyer, recorded at the county level, entirely separate from whoever farms or ranches the ground above.

Where split estate does matter for valuation is the same as it does for any mineral tract: whether there's production or drilling potential. It doesn't inherently make your minerals worth more or less than if you also owned the surface, it's simply a separate ownership structure that's extremely normal across this part of the state.

sections.title: Figuring out your specific split
sections.html: If you're not sure whether your family's minerals were split from the surface, or when, the original patent or deed at the county clerk and recorder's office will usually show the reservation language. Send us what you have and we can help make sense of it and tell you what it means for a lease or sale conversation.

faqs.q: If you own minerals but not the surface, can you visit or access the land?
faqs.a: Mineral ownership alone doesn't grant general access or recreational rights to the surface; that stays with the surface owner. Your rights are specifically tied to exploring for and producing the minerals, typically exercised through a lessee rather than personally.

faqs.q: Does the surface owner get any say in whether you lease or sell your minerals?
faqs.a: No. The mineral estate and surface estate are independently owned and transacted. The surface owner is generally notified and compensated if drilling activity affects their land, but they don't have approval rights over your leasing or selling decision.

faqs.q: How can you find out if your Montana minerals were split from the surface at some point?
faqs.a: The original patent or a subsequent deed in the county clerk's records will typically show the reservation language that created the split, and roughly when it happened.

faqs.q: Does owning both surface and minerals make your interest worth more?
faqs.a: Not necessarily for the mineral value itself, mineral value is driven by production and drilling potential regardless of who owns the surface. Owning both simply means fewer parties involved if a well is ever planned.

image.alt: Surface vs. Mineral Estate mineral rights

items.name: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI)
items.meta: Own an overriding royalty interest tied to a Montana lease? A retired operator explains what makes ORRI different, including the expiration risk owners often miss.

sections.html:
An overriding royalty interest pays like a mineral royalty but dies with the lease, and that's the one detail owners of ORRI most often don't realize until it's too late to do anything about it.

An overriding royalty interest, ORRI, is a royalty carved out of a specific oil and gas lease rather than out of the underlying mineral estate itself. Landmen, geologists, and brokers commonly receive ORRIs as part of their compensation for putting a deal together, and sometimes a mineral owner assigns part of their own interest as an ORRI to someone else as part of a transaction. Whatever the origin, the defining feature is the same: it's attached to that particular lease, not to the minerals forever.

That distinction matters enormously. Unlike mineral rights or a royalty interest carved from the mineral estate, which continue as long as you own them regardless of what happens with any given lease, an ORRI expires when the lease it's tied to expires or terminates. If that well stops producing and the lease lapses, your override goes with it, even though the underlying minerals themselves might get leased again to someone else down the road.

sections.title: Why an ORRI is fundamentally lease-dependent
sections.html:
Because an ORRI is carved from the lease rather than the mineral estate, its lifespan is tied entirely to that lease staying in effect, which in Montana usually means the well needs to keep producing in paying quantities, or the lease needs to be held by production some other way specified in its terms. Once the well stops producing and the lease terminates, the ORRI terminates too. There's no automatic renewal, and no claim against a future lease on the same acreage unless a new ORRI is separately negotiated.

This is the single biggest thing to understand before valuing or selling an ORRI: you're not buying or selling a permanent piece of the minerals, you're buying or selling a royalty stream that has a real, sometimes hard-to-predict end date tied to a specific well's productive life.

sections.title: How that changes valuation compared to mineral royalty
sections.html:
Because the income stream has a finite, well-tied horizon rather than a perpetual claim on the minerals, an ORRI generally gets valued more like an annuity against the well's remaining decline curve than like a mineral interest with open-ended upside from future re-leasing or additional wells. A buyer looking at your ORRI is really underwriting how many more years that specific well is likely to produce, and at what declining volumes, rather than the long-run potential of the whole section.

If the well is early in its life with a long runway ahead, that supports a stronger valuation. If it's a mature well deep into decline, the remaining income stream is smaller and shorter, and the offer should reflect that honestly rather than being priced as if it were a perpetual interest.

sections.title: Where Montana ORRIs commonly come from
sections.html:
We see these most often from two sources: someone who worked as a landman or broker on a deal and took part of their fee as an override rather than cash, or a mineral owner who assigned a small override to a family member or business partner as part of a prior transaction. If you inherited an ORRI without much context, checking the original assignment document, which should be recorded at the county clerk's office alongside the lease, will tell you which lease it's tied to and its specific fraction.

It's worth confirming this detail early, because an ORRI holder who mistakenly believes they hold a permanent mineral royalty can be caught off guard when a lease terminates and the payments simply stop with no recourse.

sections.title: Getting an ORRI reviewed
sections.html: Send the assignment document or division order identifying your override and the specific lease and well it's attached to. We'll look at the well's current production and estimated remaining life to give you an honest read on what the remaining income stream is worth today.

faqs.q: Does your overriding royalty interest last forever like mineral rights?
faqs.a: No. An ORRI is tied to a specific lease and ends when that lease terminates, typically when the well stops producing in paying quantities. It does not automatically transfer to a future lease on the same acreage.

faqs.q: How do you find out how much longer the well tied to your ORRI is expected to produce?
faqs.a: Recent production data and decline trends from the operator or state records give a reasonable estimate, though it's not an exact science. We look at this directly when reviewing an ORRI to give a realistic sense of remaining value.

faqs.q: Is an ORRI the same thing as an NPRI?
faqs.a: No, though they're often confused. An NPRI is carved from the mineral estate itself and can outlive any individual lease. An ORRI is carved from a specific lease and expires with it. Which one you have depends on the original document creating the interest.

faqs.q: Can you get a new override if this well's lease eventually terminates?
faqs.a: Only if you separately negotiate a new assignment on a future lease, there's no automatic right to one. This is worth keeping in mind when deciding whether to sell now or hold through the remainder of the current lease's life.

image.alt: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI) mineral rights

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: Hold a working interest in a Montana well instead of a royalty? A retired operator explains the cost exposure, why it's different from mineral rights, and how it's valued.

sections.html:
A working interest pays more per barrel than a royalty, and costs you more per dry hole. That tradeoff is the entire story, and a lot of owners only learn it from the cost statement.

A working interest is fundamentally different from the royalty and mineral interests most Montana owners hold. Where a royalty owner receives their share of production income free of drilling and operating costs, a working interest owner shares in both the production revenue and the actual costs of drilling, completing, and operating the well, proportional to their percentage. That means a bigger potential upside per barrel, but also real exposure if a well underperforms or costs run over.

Working interests in Montana usually end up in individual hands through a few paths: someone who was directly involved in putting together a drilling deal, an inheritance from a family member who invested in oil and gas operations, or occasionally a small non-operated stake bought as an investment. If you've received a joint interest billing statement, JIB, rather than just a royalty statement, you're dealing with a working interest, not a royalty.

sections.title: Why working interest income and cost exposure differ from royalty
sections.html:
As a working interest owner, your monthly or periodic statement, the joint interest billing, shows your share of both revenue and your share of costs, drilling, completion, and ongoing lease operating expenses, netted against each other. In a strong-producing well, that can mean meaningfully higher net income than an equivalent royalty percentage would provide, since you're not giving up a royalty fraction to the operator. In a weak or declining well, or if the operator needs to fund a workover or additional completion work, you can actually owe money against your interest rather than receive a check.

This cost exposure is the single biggest difference from mineral or royalty ownership, and it's worth understanding clearly before deciding whether to hold or sell a working interest. Some owners are comfortable with that risk in exchange for higher potential returns; others would rather trade it for the predictability of a royalty-style payout or a lump sum sale.

sections.title: Operated versus non-operated working interests
sections.html:
Most individual working interest owners hold a non-operated position, meaning another company, the operator, runs day-to-day decisions on the well while you simply share proportionally in the results. You don't typically get a vote on operational decisions unless your interest is unusually large, but you do receive the JIB statements and are contractually obligated for your share of approved costs under the joint operating agreement governing the well.

Understanding whether your interest is operated by a company with a strong track record in the basin, or a smaller operator with less consistent activity, matters more here than it does for a simple royalty interest, since operator competence directly affects both your revenue and your cost exposure.

sections.title: How working interests get valued for a sale
sections.html:
Valuing a working interest requires looking at both sides of the ledger: expected future revenue based on the well's decline curve and commodity price assumptions, and expected future costs, both ongoing operating expenses and any anticipated capital work like workovers or additional completions. Because of that cost exposure, working interest valuations tend to be more complex than a royalty interest, and a buyer will typically want to see recent JIB statements alongside production data to understand the full net picture rather than gross revenue alone.

Selling a working interest also transfers your obligation for future costs to the buyer along with the revenue rights, which for some owners is itself a meaningful reason to sell, particularly if a well is aging and facing higher-cost decisions ahead.

sections.title: Getting a working interest reviewed
sections.html: Send recent joint interest billing statements along with whatever operating agreement or assignment documentation you have. We'll look at both the revenue and cost side honestly and give you a real picture of what the interest is worth and what risk comes with continuing to hold it.

faqs.q: Can you lose money owning a working interest?
faqs.a: Yes, that's the key difference from a royalty interest. If a well requires costly workover or completion work, or if operating expenses exceed revenue in a given period, a working interest owner can owe money rather than receive a check.

faqs.q: What's a joint interest billing statement?
faqs.a: It's the periodic statement showing your share of both the well's revenue and its costs, drilling, completion, and operating expenses, netted against your working interest percentage. It's the working interest equivalent of a royalty statement, but with cost exposure included.

faqs.q: If you sell your working interest, do you also transfer the cost obligations?
faqs.a: Yes. The buyer takes on both the future revenue rights and the future cost obligations tied to the interest, which is part of why some owners choose to sell aging or high-maintenance working interests rather than continue absorbing that risk.

faqs.q: Is a working interest the same thing as a royalty interest?
faqs.a: No. A royalty interest receives income free of drilling and operating costs. A working interest shares proportionally in both revenue and costs. They're valued differently and carry very different risk profiles.

basins.title: Montana Basins

items.name: Bakken Mineral Rights
items.meta: Own Bakken minerals in Montana, from Elm Coulee to Richland County. A former operator explains western-flank economics and what your interest is worth.

sections.html:
The Bakken didn't stop at the state line, but the map most buyers quote from does.

We spent years on the operations side watching where rigs went and, just as often, where they didn't. When people hear Bakken they picture the Williston core in North Dakota, Mountrail, McKenzie, the counties where a single well can carry ten figures of reserves. Montana's piece of the play is real, but it's a different animal. Elm Coulee, in Richland and Sheridan County, was actually one of the original Bakken discoveries back in the early 2000s, before the horizontal completions in North Dakota made the play famous. That history matters less to buyers today than current well economics do.

If you hold minerals under acreage in Richland, Roosevelt, Sheridan, or Dawson County, you're on the western flank of the Williston Basin. That means shallower Bakken and Three Forks intervals, generally thinner pay, and operators who allocate capital here only when it competes favorably against the core. None of that makes your interest worthless, Elm Coulee has produced for two decades, but it changes how a buyer prices it and how patient you should be about timing a sale.

sections.title: Elm Coulee and the western Williston flank
sections.html:
Elm Coulee field sits mostly in Richland County, spilling into Sheridan and Roosevelt. It was drilled on the middle Bakken bench using horizontal wells before the technique spread east, and a lot of those original wellbores are now decades into their decline curve. What that means for a mineral owner: this is largely a mature, producing area rather than a frontier one. Royalty checks from Elm Coulee wells tend to be steady and modest rather than the volatile early-life numbers you see on a fresh North Dakota completion, which actually makes valuing the interest more predictable, not less.

The Three Forks bench, stacked below the middle Bakken, gets tested here too, though less densely than in McKenzie or Williams County. If your division order references both Bakken and Three Forks completions on the same or adjacent sections, that's a sign of a multi-bench operator plan, and it's worth noting when you talk to a buyer, since it can support a firmer number even on flank acreage.

sections.title: Why edge-of-play pricing differs from a straight discount
sections.html:
Buyers who work this basin daily quote core Bakken acreage against thick pay, high initial production, and a deep multi-year drilling inventory. Montana flank acreage gets quoted against thinner intervals and a shorter visible inventory, but also against lower well costs and, often, less competition for the same tract of minerals. Depending on which section you're in and whether it's held by production from an active well, offers can vary widely, and anyone quoting a flat statewide number without asking your section and township hasn't looked at your actual position.

We'd rather tell a Richland County owner the truth than a rosy number. If your minerals sit under a producing Elm Coulee well with fifteen-plus years of history, you're buying stability, and a buyer will price that against your trailing royalty checks more than against future drilling hope. If you're in an undrilled section nearby with only lease bonus history, the value leans much more heavily on whether an operator has any near-term plan for that acreage, which is a harder thing to price and worth asking about directly.

sections.title: Split estate and BLM considerations on Bakken acreage
sections.html:
A meaningful share of eastern Montana mineral ownership traces back to homestead-era patents that reserved minerals to the federal government, or to state school trust sections scattered through the townships. If your minerals are BLM-administered, any lease or sale process runs through federal record systems rather than just the county clerk's office, and title work takes longer. It's not a dealbreaker for a sale, but it's something to disclose up front, since a buyer who finds out mid-transaction that the interest is federally administered rather than fee simple will slow down and likely revise their number.

Split estate, where you own minerals but someone else owns the surface, is common across this part of Montana from old land patents. It rarely affects value directly, since royalty flows from production regardless of surface ownership, but it can affect access negotiations if a well needs to be sited on your former homestead ground. Worth knowing your own history there before you're asked.

sections.title: Getting your Elm Coulee or Bakken interest reviewed
sections.html: The fastest way to get a real number, not a mailer guess, is to send your most recent division order and a couple of royalty statements. That tells us the operator, the well, and roughly where you sit on the decline curve, which matters more on flank acreage than the county name alone does. We'll tell you plainly if we think you should hold rather than sell; that's happened more than once with owners sitting on newer completions still climbing their production curve.

faqs.q: Is Montana Bakken acreage worth less than North Dakota Bakken acreage?
faqs.a: Generally the flank commands a lower multiple of royalty income than the Williston core, but it depends heavily on your specific section, a producing Elm Coulee tract with a long payment history can outprice an undrilled North Dakota parcel with no wells nearby. Ask for a section-specific look rather than trusting a basin-wide rule of thumb.

faqs.q: Your minerals are under a well that has been producing since the early 2000s. Is it too old to matter?
faqs.a: No, a long production history is actually useful, since it gives a buyer real decline data to price against instead of guessing. Older Elm Coulee wells still on the books usually pay smaller, steadier checks, which some owners prefer to sell for a lump sum and others prefer to keep for the ongoing income. It depends on your goals.

faqs.q: How do you know if your minerals are BLM or fee simple?
faqs.a: Check your deed history or ask the county clerk's office where your patent originated; a federal mineral reservation will show up in the original patent language. If you're not sure, send us what you have and we can help you figure out which category you're in before we talk numbers.

faqs.q: What documents speed up a Bakken mineral review?
faqs.a: A recent division order, one or two royalty check stubs, and your deed or probate document if the interest passed to you that way. With those three, we can usually give you a real range within a couple of days rather than a generic estimate.

items.name: Powder River Basin Mineral Rights
items.meta: Coalbed methane, Big George coal, and scattered oil tests on the Montana side of the Powder River Basin. A retired operator explains what's active and how CBM royalty differs.

sections.html:
Most of what gets drilled in the Powder River Basin is south of the state line, but Montana's corner has its own story, coal gas first, oil a distant second.

The Powder River Basin is really two basins depending on who's talking to you. In Wyoming it's coalbed methane country, thousands of shallow wells producing gas out of the Big George and other Fort Union coal seams. In Montana, mostly Powder River and Carter County, the play never reached that same density, but there was a real coalbed methane boom here in the early 2000s that put a lot of wells on the ground and a lot of royalty owners on division orders they still hold today.

If your minerals sit in southeastern Montana and your family has ever mentioned CBM or coalbed gas, that's almost certainly what you're dealing with rather than a conventional oil play. It changes how we'd value your interest and what questions we'd ask before quoting you anything.

sections.title: Coalbed methane is a different economic animal than shale oil
sections.html:
CBM wells are shallow, cheap to drill, and produce gas at low pressure by first pumping water off the coal seam to release the methane. That means early production often looks backwards from an oil well, gas volumes climb for a while as the coal dewaters, then decline. If you've been getting small, somewhat unpredictable royalty checks that don't match a typical oil decline curve, that's normal for CBM, not a sign something's wrong with your interest.

The economics also depend heavily on natural gas prices, which have been weak for stretches over the last decade. A lot of Powder River CBM wells in Montana were shut in or plugged when gas prices dropped, and some interests that were producing in 2008 are sitting non-producing now. That doesn't erase the value of your mineral position, but it does mean a buyer will look hard at whether there's any current production, any recent workover activity, or any signal the operator plans to come back.

sections.title: Carter and Powder River County ownership patterns
sections.html:
This part of Montana was homesteaded later and more sparsely than the wheat country further north, and a lot of the original patents split minerals from surface at statehood or through federal land grants. Split estate is common, and BLM administers a real share of the mineral base in this corner of the state. If your family's ownership traces to an old homestead patent, expect the title chain to run through both county records and, in some cases, federal land office records.

Fractional ownership is also common here because these interests have been passed down through two or three generations without much consolidation. If you own a small undivided percentage rather than a whole tract, that's typical for this basin and doesn't disqualify you from a sale, it just means the buyer needs your exact decimal interest from a division order to quote accurately.

sections.title: What actually moves value in this basin
sections.html:
Three things matter more here than in an oil-focused basin: whether the well is currently producing, what gas price the operator is realizing net of gathering and compression deductions, and whether there's any nearby permitting activity suggesting renewed interest. Coal seam gas plays can see episodic revivals when prices recover, so an interest that looks quiet today isn't necessarily done for good. We'd rather look at your actual check history than guess off a basin-wide average, since CBM economics vary section to section more than a conventional play does.

Oil tests do happen in this corner of the basin too, mostly shallower conventional targets rather than a horizontal shale program, and those interests get valued more like a traditional stripper-well royalty than a CBM interest. Know which one you actually hold before comparing notes with a neighbor.

sections.title: Reviewing a Powder River Basin interest
sections.html: Send your division order and the most recent statements you have, even if the checks have been small or the well looks shut in. Gas deduction lines on a CBM statement can be confusing, transportation, compression, and gathering fees eat into the wellhead price in ways that aren't always obvious, and we can walk you through what you're actually being paid net of those deductions before we talk about a sale number.

faqs.q: Why are your Powder River Basin royalty checks so small compared to what you hear about the Bakken?
faqs.a: Coalbed methane wells produce gas, not oil, at lower per-unit value and often with heavier deductions for gathering and compression. Small, steady checks are typical for this play and don't necessarily mean your interest is worth little, it's just a different production profile than an oil well.

faqs.q: Your CBM well hasn't produced in years. Is your mineral interest still worth anything?
faqs.a: Often yes. A shut-in or plugged well doesn't erase future value if gas prices recover or an operator decides to re-enter the field. Buyers price non-producing interests more conservatively, but they're rarely worthless, especially if there's still infrastructure nearby.

faqs.q: How do gas deductions on your division order work?
faqs.a: Operators typically net transportation, compression, and sometimes processing fees against the wellhead price before calculating your royalty. Two owners with the same decimal interest can see different net checks depending on the pipeline and gathering arrangement for their specific well.

faqs.q: What if you only own a small fractional interest inherited from a grandparent?
faqs.a: That's the norm in this basin. Send whatever division order or probate paperwork you have and we can usually trace the decimal interest even from an old or partial document.

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A step-by-step walkthrough of selling mineral rights in Montana, written by a retired E&P engineer who now buys interests directly from owners.

sections.html:
Selling mineral rights isn't complicated once you know the sequence, but most owners go into it not knowing what order things actually happen in.

We've been on both sides of this transaction, running production for operators for years and now buying interests directly, and the process itself is fairly straightforward once you strip away the confusion. What trips owners up is not knowing what to expect at each step, so they either move too fast on a bad offer or sit on a good one out of uncertainty.

Here's the process the way it actually unfolds for a Montana owner, not the marketing version.

sections.title: Start With What You Actually Own
sections.html:
Before anything else, confirm exactly what interest you hold: mineral rights, royalty interest, or both, and whether it's producing or non-producing. Pull your deed and, if the tract is producing, your most recent royalty statements. This sounds basic, but we've talked to owners who assumed they owned a full mineral interest when in fact they only held a royalty carved out of someone else's minerals, which changes everything about how the tract gets valued.

If you're not certain, a county title search will settle it, and it's worth doing before you start collecting offers rather than after.

sections.title: Get Real Numbers On The Table
sections.html:
Once ownership is clear, share your decimal interest, county location, and recent production history with whoever you're talking to, and expect a real offer to be built from that, not quoted off a general per-acre range you saw advertised somewhere. In Montana, an interest near active Bakken flank drilling gets valued differently than an older, low-volume Cut Bank interest, so location and recent activity genuinely change the number.

It's reasonable to get more than one offer. What matters is comparing them on the same basis, meaning the same decimal interest and the same understanding of whether the tract is producing or not.

sections.title: Vet The Buyer Before You Vet The Offer
sections.html:
A legitimate buyer will ask for documentation, explain how they arrived at their number, and give you time to review the purchase agreement, ideally with your own attorney if the transaction is at all complicated. Be wary of anyone pushing you to sign the same day, quoting a number with no supporting documents requested, or refusing to explain their math. Those are the tells of a lowball operation, not a serious buyer.

You're also entitled to ask how the closing will actually work, who's preparing the deed, and where the money comes from, before you commit to anything.

sections.title: Closing Without Surprises
sections.html:
A clean closing involves a purchase and sale agreement, a mineral deed transferring the interest, and typically a title company or attorney handling the actual closing and recording with the county clerk and recorder. Funds are usually released once the deed is signed, notarized, and confirmed for recording, not before. If there's an unresolved heirship or title issue, expect that to be sorted out as part of closing rather than something that kills the deal outright.

Once recorded, the new owner is responsible for updating the operator's division order records, which is worth confirming happens rather than assuming it does automatically.

faqs.q: How long does selling mineral rights usually take in Montana?
faqs.a: With clean title and complete documents, a straightforward sale can close within a few weeks. Unresolved heirship or a missing legal description can extend that timeline.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell all of your mineral interest, or can you sell part?
faqs.a: You can typically sell a portion of your interest and retain the rest, though this should be spelled out clearly in the deed to avoid confusion about what was actually conveyed.

faqs.q: What if you only own a small fractional interest inherited from family?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests are common in Montana due to generations of inherited land, and they're still sellable. The offer simply reflects your actual decimal share, not a full mineral acre.

faqs.q: Can you back out after signing a purchase agreement?
faqs.a: That depends entirely on the terms of the specific agreement you signed, which is exactly why reading it carefully, or having an attorney review it, matters before you sign.

faqs.q: Do you need to be present in Montana to close the sale?
faqs.a: No, most closings are handled by mail or courier with notarized documents, so an out-of-state owner can complete the sale without traveling.

faqs.q: What if you get an offer and you're still not sure whether to sell?
faqs.a: A real offer doesn't expire in a day. Take it to a family member, an attorney, or simply sit with it for a week before deciding. Any buyer worth working with expects that and won't pressure you off a considered decision.

faqs.q: Does selling require you to hire your own landman or title researcher?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. A serious buyer typically handles or coordinates the title work as part of the transaction, though you're always free to have your own attorney review anything before you sign.

faqs.q: What's the biggest mistake owners make when selling for the first time?
faqs.a: Accepting the first number without asking how it was calculated or comparing it to anything else. Even a fair offer is worth understanding before you sign, and a legitimate buyer will never treat that request as unreasonable.

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: A former operations engineer explains, in plain terms, what actually drives mineral rights value in Montana, from Bakken flank position to split estate status.

sections.html:
There is no single number that answers this question honestly, and anyone who quotes you one over the phone without seeing your tract is guessing.

We spent decades on the operating side before we started buying interests directly from owners, and the question we get asked first, almost every time, is what a tract is worth. The honest answer is that value depends on a handful of specific factors, and once you understand them you can at least tell whether an offer is in a reasonable range for your situation.

This guide walks through what actually moves the number for Montana owners specifically, since our geology and land patterns are different from Texas or Oklahoma in ways that matter.

sections.title: Why Position On The Play Moves The Number
sections.html:
Montana sits on the western edge of the Bakken and Three Forks trend, and the difference between a tract near the North Dakota line in Richland or Sheridan County and one further west toward Fallon or Wibaux can be significant. Core acreage with dense, prolific horizontal wells commands a stronger multiple against current royalty income than flank acreage where wells are sparser and less predictable. Neither is worthless, but they are not priced the same way, and any buyer who quotes you the same range for both hasn't actually looked at where your tract sits.

Central Montana's older Sweetgrass Arch and Cut Bank fields are a different animal entirely, generally lower-volume, longer-life stripper production that gets valued more on steady cash flow than on drilling upside.

sections.title: Producing Versus Non-Producing Minerals
sections.html:
A producing interest with real royalty history is far easier to value than raw, undeveloped minerals with no well ever drilled on them. Producing value is typically quoted as a multiple of recent monthly or annual net royalty, adjusted for expected decline, so recent statements matter enormously here. Non-producing minerals depend almost entirely on whether the tract sits in an area operators are actively leasing, which in Montana can shift with commodity prices and drilling budgets from one year to the next.

If you haven't received a check in years and there's no active leasing nearby, value is going to reflect speculative, longer-term potential rather than anything close to current income.

sections.title: Federal Versus Fee Minerals In Montana
sections.html:
Montana has a meaningful amount of federally administered minerals, particularly where homestead-era patents severed the mineral estate from the surface, and around tribal and BLM-managed land. Federal minerals operate under different leasing rules, royalty rates, and timelines than privately held fee minerals, and that affects how a buyer prices them. It isn't automatically worse, but it typically means longer holding periods before development and different administrative overhead, which a buyer has to account for in the number they offer.

If you aren't sure whether your interest is fee or federal, your original deed or patent, along with a title search, will usually settle it.

sections.title: What Actually Sets A Buyer's Offer
sections.html:
In practice, an offer typically gets built from your decimal interest, recent net royalty if the tract is producing, an assumed decline rate based on comparable wells nearby, and a risk-adjusted multiple that reflects how confident the buyer is in future drilling. Values move with oil and gas prices and with how active operators are in your specific township and range, which is why a number that seemed low two years ago might look different today, and vice versa.

Nobody honest can hand you a firm price without seeing your decimal interest, recent statements, and county location, so treat any unsolicited number that arrives before those documents are reviewed as a starting point for conversation, rather than a real offer.

faqs.q: Can you just tell you a dollar amount per acre over the phone?
faqs.a: No, and you should be skeptical of anyone who does. A real number depends on your decimal interest, whether the tract is producing, and recent activity nearby, all of which take a look at your documents to assess.

faqs.q: Are non-producing minerals worth anything in Montana?
faqs.a: They can be, especially near active drilling areas along the Bakken flank, but the value reflects speculative future development rather than current income, so it is typically a smaller number than a producing tract.

faqs.q: Does having federal or BLM-administered minerals lower the value?
faqs.a: Not automatically, but it does change the timeline and administrative process, which buyers factor into what they offer. Fee and federal minerals are simply priced under different assumptions.

faqs.q: Why would two neighboring tracts get different offers?
faqs.a: Small differences in decimal interest, well spacing, lease terms, or which side of a unit boundary a tract falls on can produce noticeably different valuations even for adjacent land.

faqs.q: What documents should you have ready before asking for a real number?
faqs.a: Your deed or patent, recent royalty statements if the tract is producing, and any division order paperwork give a buyer enough to put together an informed, tract-specific offer.

faqs.q: Does an older lease with a low royalty rate hurt your value today?
faqs.a: It can, since a low legacy royalty rate reduces your net revenue from any given well, which flows directly into the income approach a buyer uses on producing minerals.
