items.name: Reading Your Royalty Statements
items.meta: A retired E&P engineer explains what each line on a Montana royalty statement means, why the check shrinks over time, and when the numbers signal a sale.

sections.html:
Most owners we talk to have a drawer full of royalty stubs they have never actually read line by line. Here is what the paper is telling you.

We ran production for a good chunk of our career before we started buying mineral interests instead of operating them, and one thing never changed: owners get a statement every month and most of them file it without reading it. That is a mistake, because the statement is the only document that tells you, in real numbers, what your interest is actually doing right now, not what a landman told you it might do ten years ago.

This is written for Montana owners specifically, because a lot of the interests up here sit on the flank of the Bakken or in older Sweetgrass Arch and Cut Bank production, and the statement math behaves differently depending on where your tract sits.

sections.title: What Shows Up On The Check Stub
sections.html:
A royalty statement is going to list a well or lease name, a production month, gross volumes of oil and gas, your decimal interest, price received, deductions, and severance and production taxes withheld before you ever see the money. Montana withholds its own production tax at the source, so the number on your stub is already net of that. If you are comparing your check to a neighbor's or to something you read online, make sure you are comparing net figures to net figures, not gross production to a net check.

The decimal interest line is the one owners skip past fastest and it is the one that matters most. That number represents your fractional share of the well after unitization, and if you inherited a piece of a larger family tract, it can look startlingly small even when the well itself is producing well.

sections.title: Interest Type And Why It Matters
sections.html:
Whether you hold a royalty interest, an overriding royalty, or a working interest changes what deductions legally apply to you. Straight royalty owners in Montana are typically shielded from post-production costs by lease language more often than not, but we have seen enough leases from the 1970s and 1980s with weak proceeds language that deductions crept in anyway. If your net number has dropped and gross production hasn't, that is the first thing worth checking against your actual lease.

Working interest owners, which is a smaller group but not a rare one on old Montana leases, see their own operating costs subtracted before anything reaches them, which is a very different statement to read than a royalty owner's.

sections.title: Reading The Decline Behind The Numbers
sections.html:
Wells on the edge of the Bakken in eastern Montana, out around Richland, Roosevelt, and McCone counties, tend to decline faster in year one and two than the type curves people quote you make it sound. A well that opened strong can be down forty to sixty percent within eighteen months, then settle into a long, shallow tail that produces modest but steady royalty for years. If your statement shows a steep drop after a hot first year, that is normal decline behavior, not a sign anything is wrong with the well.

Older Cut Bank and Sweetgrass Arch production in the northern part of the state behaves differently: shallower declines, but lower absolute volumes from the start. Knowing which kind of well sits under your tract changes how you should read a falling number.

sections.title: When The Numbers Don't Match What You Expected
sections.html:
If a check stops arriving entirely, the most common cause isn't fraud, it is a title problem: a name doesn't match county records, an heirship chain was never cleaned up, or an address change never made it to the operator's division order department. Before you assume the worst, pull your last several statements and check whether your decimal interest itself changed, which usually points to a spacing unit adjustment or a new well entering the unit.

This is also the point where a lot of owners start thinking about selling rather than continuing to track a declining, sometimes confusing income stream, and that's a reasonable thing to weigh once you actually understand what the statement is telling you.

faqs.q: Why did your royalty check drop by half after the first year?
faqs.a: That is typical decline curve behavior for a horizontal well on the edge of the Bakken. Production is highest in the first several months and falls off quickly before settling into a longer, shallower tail.

faqs.q: What is the difference between gross and net volumes on your statement?
faqs.a: Gross is the well's total production; net is your decimal share after deductions and taxes. Always compare net figures when checking your numbers against someone else's, since gross tells you nothing about your actual interest.

faqs.q: Why is Montana production tax already taken out of your check?
faqs.a: Montana withholds oil and gas production tax at the source, so the amount on your statement is already net of that state tax, unlike some other states where you handle it separately at filing time.

faqs.q: Your decimal interest changed between statements. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Yes, this usually happens when a new well is added to your spacing unit or a unit boundary is adjusted, which dilutes or increases each owner's fractional share depending on direction.

faqs.q: Should you still be tracking statements if you're thinking about selling?
faqs.a: Recent statements are one of the first things a buyer will ask for, since they show current decimal interest and recent net revenue, which anchors any offer to real, current activity rather than guesswork.

image.alt: Reading Your Royalty Statements mineral rights

items.name: Division Orders Explained
items.meta: A retired operations engineer breaks down what a division order actually is, how your decimal interest gets calculated, and common Montana title snags.

sections.html:
A division order lands in your mailbox with a well name and a decimal you've never seen before, and most owners just sign it without asking where that number came from.

We spent years on the operator side preparing these things before we ever bought a mineral interest ourselves, so we've seen a division order from both directions. It is not a lease and it does not transfer ownership of anything, but it is the document that tells the company how to split your royalty check, and getting it wrong costs owners real money.

Montana owners run into a specific set of complications here, mostly tied to heirship and old family land that was never formally divided on paper, so this is worth understanding before you sign anything.

sections.title: What A Division Order Actually Does
sections.html:
A division order is the operator's statement of who owns what percentage of production from a specific well, and it authorizes the company to pay you according to that decimal. It is built from the title work the operator or a title company did on the spacing unit, and it is meant to match your deed, not create new rights. Signing it does not waive any claim you have to your actual mineral ownership; it simply confirms how the operator will distribute the check.

That said, if the decimal is wrong and you sign without checking, correcting it later can take months, during which your check may be held in suspense or split incorrectly.

sections.title: How Your Decimal Interest Gets Calculated
sections.html:
Your decimal comes from your net mineral acres divided by the total acreage in the spacing unit, multiplied by the royalty rate in your lease. A Montana spacing unit for a horizontal Bakken well commonly runs 1,280 acres, so even a full mineral acre or two nets you a small decimal once it's spread across the whole unit and multiple owners. This is exactly why an inherited fractional interest, say a sixteenth passed down through two generations, can look like an oddly specific, small number on the page.

If your acreage figure on the division order doesn't match your deed, that mismatch is worth catching before you sign, not after the first check arrives short.

sections.title: Common Snags On Montana Titles
sections.html:
The most frequent problem we see on Montana division orders traces back to heirship: a mineral owner passed away decades ago, the interest was never run through probate or a clean chain of title, and the family has been splitting checks informally, or not receiving them at all because the operator has the interest held in suspense under the deceased owner's name. Operators generally will not issue a division order to heirs without a probate decree, affidavit of heirship, or similar document establishing the current legal owners.

Old homestead-era severed mineral tracts add another wrinkle, since some of these were divided among multiple heirs generations back with no modern survey, leaving legal descriptions that require careful reconciliation against current county records.

sections.title: What Happens If You Don't Sign
sections.html:
You are not legally required to sign a division order to retain your ownership, but most operators will hold your royalty in suspense until you do, meaning no checks go out. If something on the form looks off, the right move is to contact the operator's division order department directly, not only sign and hope, since a wrong decimal that goes uncorrected for years can be a genuine headache to unwind.

For owners weighing a sale, a current, signed division order with a confirmed decimal is one of the cleanest pieces of proof a buyer can use to move quickly on an offer.

faqs.q: Is a division order the same thing as a lease?
faqs.a: No. A lease grants drilling rights to an operator; a division order simply tells the operator how to split the royalty check among current owners. They are separate documents with different purposes.

faqs.q: What happens if you never sign your division order?
faqs.a: The operator typically holds your royalty in suspense rather than paying you, until the paperwork is resolved. Your underlying ownership isn't affected, but you won't see checks in the meantime.

faqs.q: Why is your decimal interest such a small, specific number?
faqs.a: It reflects your net mineral acres divided across the full spacing unit, which in Montana often runs 1,280 acres for a horizontal well, then further divided if your interest passed through multiple generations of heirs.

faqs.q: Your relative passed away and the well is still under their name. What now?
faqs.a: The operator generally needs a probate decree or affidavit of heirship establishing current ownership before it will issue a new division order and release held funds to the rightful heirs.

faqs.q: Should you sign a division order before or after selling your minerals?
faqs.a: A current, accurate division order actually helps a sale move faster, since it confirms your decimal interest with documentation a buyer can rely on rather than estimate.

faqs.q: Can an operator change your decimal interest without notifying you first?
faqs.a: They shouldn't. A new or corrected division order should be sent for your review whenever your interest changes, whether from a new well entering the unit or a title correction, and you're entitled to ask questions before signing.

image.alt: Division Orders Explained mineral rights

items.name: Documents You Need to Sell
items.meta: What paperwork a buyer actually needs to make a real offer on Montana minerals, including split estate and federal surface records, from a former operator.

sections.html:
Owners lose weeks waiting on paperwork they didn't know they needed. Here is the real list, in the order it usually gets requested.

After years of pulling title on Montana tracts, both as an operator and now as a buyer, we can tell you the offer process moves at the speed of your paperwork, nothing else. Most delays aren't about negotiating price, they're about someone digging through a filing cabinet for a deed that's been misplaced since a parent's estate closed.

This is the list we actually ask for, roughly in the order it matters, along with why each piece counts.

sections.title: The Paper Trail A Buyer Needs
sections.html:
Start with your deed or the document that shows how you acquired the mineral interest, whether that's a warranty deed, a mineral deed, or a patent if it traces back to an original federal land grant. Alongside that, a legal description of the tract, meaning the section, township, and range, is what actually identifies the property in county records, not a mailing address or a rough sense of where the land sits.

If the tract is producing, recent royalty statements and, if you have it, a copy of your division order round out the core package and let a buyer confirm your decimal interest without waiting on a fresh title run.

sections.title: Title And Heirship Documents
sections.html:
If you inherited the interest, whatever settled the estate matters: a probate decree, a will, or an affidavit of heirship if the estate was small enough to bypass formal probate under Montana law. Many Montana families hold minerals that passed down two or three generations without ever being run through a full title update, and a buyer will need to see how ownership moved from the original owner to you specifically before closing.

If there's any question about who else might share the interest, siblings, cousins, or other heirs, it's worth sorting that out early rather than discovering a co-owner mid-transaction.

sections.title: Split Estate And Federal Surface Records
sections.html:
A fair number of Montana tracts are split estate, meaning the mineral rights and surface rights are owned separately, often because a homestead-era patent reserved minerals to the federal government while granting surface to a private settler, or the reverse happened through a later severance. If your minerals sit under BLM-administered surface, or your interest itself is a federal mineral lease rather than fee minerals, that status shows up in BLM or county records and changes how the transaction is structured.

It's worth knowing before you start whether you're dealing with fee minerals under private surface, fee minerals under federal surface, or a federal mineral interest outright, since each requires slightly different documentation to transfer cleanly.

sections.title: What To Do If You're Missing Something
sections.html:
Don't let a missing document stop you from starting the conversation. Most gaps, a lost deed, an unresolved heirship, an old legal description that doesn't match a modern survey, can be filled in during the process, often by the buyer's title company rather than you. County clerk and recorder offices keep public records going back generations, and a competent title search usually turns up what's missing faster than you'd expect on your own.

The one document nobody can manufacture after the fact is your identity as a legitimate owner, so as long as that's clear, the rest is administrative work, not a dealbreaker.

faqs.q: What's the single most important document to have ready?
faqs.a: Your deed or the instrument showing how you acquired the interest, along with a legal description by section, township, and range. That's what identifies the tract in county records.

faqs.q: You inherited your minerals but never went through probate. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: It can slow things down, but it isn't a dealbreaker. Montana allows affidavits of heirship for smaller estates, and a title company can often help sort out what's needed.

faqs.q: What does split estate mean for your paperwork?
faqs.a: It means your mineral rights and the surface above them are owned separately, often tracing back to a federal homestead patent. It doesn't block a sale, but the title company needs to know which situation applies to structure the transfer correctly.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to gather these documents?
faqs.a: Not necessarily to gather them, but for anything involving unresolved heirship, unclear title, or federal mineral status, it's worth talking to an attorney before signing a transfer document.

faqs.q: How long does it take to sort out missing paperwork?
faqs.a: It varies with the complexity of the title, but straightforward gaps are often resolved within a few weeks once a title search is underway, especially with county records to work from.

faqs.q: What if your mineral tract has never had a legal survey?
faqs.a: Many older Montana homestead tracts were only ever described by section, township, and range, without a modern survey, and that's typically sufficient for county records and a title company to work with, so it's rarely a reason to delay reaching out.

faqs.q: Do you need to gather every document before you make first contact?
faqs.a: No, start the conversation with whatever you have on hand, even if it's incomplete. A buyer can usually tell you exactly which specific gaps matter for your tract, which saves you from chasing paperwork you may not actually need.

image.alt: Documents You Need to Sell mineral rights

items.name: How to Spot a Lowball Offer
items.meta: A retired E&P engineer breaks down the real tells of a lowball mineral rights offer in Montana and how to compare offers on fair, equal terms.

sections.html:
After years watching offers get built on the operator side, we can usually tell within a few minutes whether a number is fair or fishing for a quick signature.

Not every low offer is dishonest, some tracts genuinely are worth less than an owner expects, and that's a fair thing to hear even if it's disappointing. But there's a real difference between a legitimately conservative offer and one built to take advantage of an owner who doesn't know what questions to ask.

This is what we've learned to watch for, on both sides of the table, specific to how these deals tend to get worked in Montana.

sections.title: The Tells we Learned To Watch For
sections.html:
A number that arrives before anyone has asked for your deed, your decimal interest, or recent royalty statements is a guess, not an offer, no matter how confidently it's presented. Real offers get built from your actual documents. Pressure to sign within twenty-four or forty-eight hours, especially paired with vague language about the offer expiring or the buyer moving on to someone else, is a classic tactic meant to prevent you from getting a second opinion or reading the paperwork carefully.

We'd also watch for anyone who won't explain how they arrived at their number when you ask directly. A legitimate buyer can walk you through their reasoning, even in general terms; someone hoping you won't look closely usually can't or won't.

sections.title: Comparing Offers Apples To Apples
sections.html:
The only fair way to compare two offers is to make sure they're valuing the same thing: the same decimal interest, the same understanding of whether the tract is producing, and clarity on whether the number is for all your minerals or only a portion. We've seen owners compare a per-acre figure from one buyer against a lump-sum figure from another without realizing they weren't measuring the same quantity at all.

If a buyer's number seems unusually high compared to everyone else, that's worth scrutinizing too, since an inflated offer sometimes comes with unfavorable terms buried elsewhere in the purchase agreement, or simply doesn't survive to closing.

sections.title: Pressure Tactics And Why They Work
sections.html:
Lowball tactics work because most owners sell a mineral interest once, maybe twice, in their lives, so there's no accumulated experience to draw on the way there would be selling a house or a car. Buyers who rely on that inexperience count on urgency and unfamiliarity doing the work that a fair number should. Family land, inherited interests especially, adds an emotional layer too, an eagerness to just be done with the paperwork and the phone calls that can make a quick, mediocre offer look more appealing than it should.

Slowing down costs you nothing. A legitimate offer will still be roughly the same, or the buyer will explain clearly why it changed, a week from now.

sections.title: What A Fair Offer Actually Looks Like
sections.html:
A fair offer requests your documents before quoting a firm number, explains its reasoning when asked, gives you real time to review the purchase agreement, and doesn't penalize you for wanting a second opinion or an attorney's review. It should also account for the specific characteristics of your tract, its play position, whether it's producing, and its decline trajectory, rather than applying a flat, generic rate regardless of where in Montana your minerals actually sit.

If you get more than one offer and they're in a reasonably similar range once adjusted for the same decimal interest, that's usually a sign the market has priced your tract fairly, even if the number is smaller than you'd hoped.

faqs.q: Is a low offer always a scam?
faqs.a: No. Some tracts are genuinely lower value, particularly non-producing minerals far from active drilling. The concern is offers built without reviewing your actual documents or delivered with heavy pressure to sign fast.

faqs.q: How many offers should you get before deciding?
faqs.a: Two or three from buyers willing to review your actual decimal interest and documents gives you a reasonable sense of the market range without dragging the process out for months.

faqs.q: What if a buyer refuses to explain how they calculated their offer?
faqs.a: That's a legitimate reason for caution. A buyer confident in their number should be able to explain the basic reasoning, even without disclosing every internal detail.

faqs.q: Should you be worried if an offer expires in 48 hours?
faqs.a: Yes, treat that as a warning sign rather than normal business practice. Real offers built from real documents don't typically require that kind of rushed decision.

faqs.q: Can you negotiate a mineral rights offer, or is it take it or leave it?
faqs.a: Most legitimate buyers expect some negotiation, particularly if you can point to specific comparable activity or documentation that supports a higher number.

faqs.q: What if a buyer's offer letter has no company name or contact information?
faqs.a: Treat that as a serious red flag. A legitimate buyer stands behind their offer with a name, a phone number, and a way to verify who you're actually dealing with before any documents get signed.

items.name: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer
items.meta: How mineral deeds and title transfer actually work in Montana, including heirship, county recording, and split estate deed language, from a former engineer.

sections.html:
A mineral deed is a short document that does a lot of legal work, and getting the wording wrong can cause title problems that outlast the person who signed it.

We've reviewed enough old Montana mineral deeds over the years, some typed on a manual typewriter decades ago, to know that small drafting choices from generations back still shape what an owner can and can't do with their interest today. Understanding what a deed actually transfers, and how title moves through the county system, helps you avoid adding to that pile of confusion.

This covers the mechanics plainly, without the legalese most owners never get walked through.

sections.title: What A Mineral Deed Actually Transfers
sections.html:
A mineral deed conveys ownership of the mineral estate, meaning the right to explore for, produce, and receive royalty from oil, gas, and typically other minerals under a described tract, separate from the surface. It should include a clear legal description by section, township, and range, the type of interest conveyed such as a full or fractional mineral interest, and whether any existing lease and its royalty obligations transfer along with it. A deed that's vague on any of these points is the kind of thing that generates disputes years down the road, often after the person who signed it is no longer around to clarify intent.

Unlike a general warranty deed on a house, mineral deeds are frequently quitclaim or special warranty in form, meaning the seller only guarantees they haven't personally clouded title, not that title is perfect against every possible claim.

sections.title: Recording It Right In The County Clerk's Office
sections.html:
Once signed and notarized, a mineral deed needs to be recorded with the clerk and recorder in the Montana county where the property sits, which is what makes the transfer part of the public record and puts future buyers, operators, and title examiners on notice of the new ownership. Recording isn't optional if you want the transfer to hold up cleanly; an unrecorded deed can create real problems if the same interest ever gets conveyed or claimed by someone else afterward.

After recording, it's the new owner's responsibility, or the buyer's in most transactions, to notify the operator's division order department so future royalty checks go to the right place instead of continuing to the seller's name.

sections.title: Heirship And Probate Complications
sections.html:
When an owner passes away without a deed already transferring their interest, ownership generally moves through their estate, either formal probate or, for smaller Montana estates, a simplified affidavit process. Until that's completed and recorded, the operator typically won't issue a new division order, and any sale has to work through the estate rather than around it. This is where a lot of the family-land situations we see in Montana get complicated, minerals split among three or four siblings or cousins none of whom have formally cleared title, sometimes going back two generations.

If you're in that position, a title attorney can usually map out the shortest path to clean, sellable title faster than trying to piece it together from old paperwork on your own.

sections.title: Split Estate Deeds And Surface Use Language
sections.html:
When minerals and surface are held by different owners, which is common across Montana due to homestead-era severances, a mineral deed should be clear that it conveys minerals only, with no claim to the surface. Some older deeds include surface use language granting the mineral owner reasonable access to explore and produce, which matters if the tract is ever leased, since that access right typically transfers with the minerals. If your minerals sit under BLM-administered surface, the transfer of a fee mineral interest doesn't touch the federal surface estate at all, those remain entirely separate ownership chains.

Knowing which situation applies to your tract before drafting a deed avoids ambiguity that could otherwise sit unresolved for years.

faqs.q: Do you need a lawyer to transfer a mineral deed in Montana?
faqs.a: It isn't legally required for a straightforward transfer, but for anything involving heirship, split estate language, or an existing lease, having an attorney review the deed is a reasonable safeguard against ambiguity.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a quitclaim and warranty mineral deed?
faqs.a: A quitclaim conveys whatever interest the seller has without guaranteeing clear title, while a warranty deed includes some level of assurance against title defects. Mineral deeds often fall somewhere between the two.

faqs.q: How long does county recording take in Montana?
faqs.a: It varies by county clerk and recorder office, but most straightforward mineral deeds are recorded within a few days to a couple of weeks after submission.

faqs.q: Your deed is unclear on whether it includes surface rights. What do you do?
faqs.a: Have a title professional or attorney review the exact language, since ambiguous surface access clauses in split estate situations are a common source of later disputes.

faqs.q: What happens if a mineral deed is never recorded?
faqs.a: The transfer may still be valid between the parties, but an unrecorded deed leaves the door open for competing claims and creates real problems if the interest is ever sold or leased again.

image.alt: Mineral Deeds & Title Transfer mineral rights

items.name: Lease vs. Sell: Which Is Right?
items.meta: A retired E&P engineer compares leasing and selling Montana mineral rights honestly, covering what each option actually commits you to long term.

sections.html:
Owners often treat this as a simple either-or question when really it depends on how much uncertainty you're willing to carry for how long.

We spent our working life on the operator side negotiating leases, and now we buy minerals outright from owners, so we've sat across the table on both kinds of deals. Neither leasing nor selling is the obviously correct choice; they trade different things for different outcomes, and the right answer depends on your specific interest and what you actually need from it.

This is the comparison we'd walk a family member through, not a pitch for one option over the other.

sections.title: What Leasing Actually Commits You To
sections.html:
Leasing means you keep ownership of the minerals but grant an operator the right to explore and produce for a set primary term, usually three to five years in Montana, in exchange for a bonus payment upfront and a royalty percentage on anything produced. You retain long-term upside if a well is drilled and performs well, but you also retain the downside: no drilling ever happens, or a well is drilled and declines faster than expected, or you're back to negotiating again once the lease term or held-by-production status runs out.

Leasing keeps you exposed to commodity price swings and operator decisions for as long as you hold the interest, which some owners want and others find exhausting to track.

sections.title: What Selling Actually Gives Up
sections.html:
Selling converts your interest into a lump sum today and permanently ends your claim to future royalty, whether the tract turns out to be worth far more or far less than expected down the road. You give up all upside from future wells, price increases, or new formations someone eventually figures out how to produce economically. In exchange, you get certainty: a fixed number, no more tracking statements, no more wondering whether a check will arrive next month.

For a producing tract already on a steep decline curve, that certainty can be worth more than continuing to collect a shrinking royalty for years.

sections.title: Where Montana Owners Get This Wrong
sections.html:
The mistake we see most is owners assuming leasing is always the safer, more conservative choice because they keep ownership. But a lease with no drilling commitment and a distant, uncertain primary term isn't actually safer than a sale, it's just a different kind of uncertainty, one where you're betting on an operator's future plans rather than locking in a known amount. On the flank of the Bakken especially, where drilling activity has been inconsistent year to year, plenty of leases have simply expired with nothing ever drilled.

On the other side, owners with strong, recently producing tracts sometimes sell too early out of a desire for simplicity, without weighing what years of remaining royalty income might have added up to.

sections.title: A Framework, Not A Formula
sections.html:
If your interest is non-producing and there's no active drilling nearby, leasing costs you little and preserves future option value. If your interest is producing but clearly on the back half of its decline curve, selling often makes more practical sense than holding out for a shrinking royalty. If you need capital now, for a health situation, a debt payoff, an inheritance split among siblings, that need itself is a legitimate factor, not something to feel embarrassed weighing against theoretical future upside.

There's no universal right answer here, only the one that fits your actual interest and your actual situation, and it's worth getting real numbers on both paths before deciding.

faqs.q: Can you lease and still sell later?
faqs.a: Yes, an unleased or currently leased mineral interest can generally still be sold, though an active lease and any related royalty obligations transfer along with the minerals to the new owner.

faqs.q: Is selling always a worse deal than leasing if a well eventually gets drilled?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. If the well underperforms or declines quickly, as many do on the edge of the Bakken, a lump sum sale can end up being the better outcome in hindsight, though nobody can know that in advance.

faqs.q: What happens to your lease if you decide to sell your minerals?
faqs.a: The lease transfers with the mineral interest to the new owner, and the buyer typically factors any existing lease terms into the offer they make you.

faqs.q: Does leasing pay anything upfront?
faqs.a: Yes, leases typically include an upfront bonus payment per acre, in addition to the royalty percentage on anything eventually produced, though bonus amounts vary with drilling interest in the area.

faqs.q: How do you know if your tract is on the back half of its decline curve?
faqs.a: Recent royalty statements showing a steady, sustained drop over multiple years, rather than a single-month dip, are the clearest sign the well has moved into its long, low-volume tail.

faqs.q: Is there a middle option between leasing and selling everything?
faqs.a: Yes, some owners sell a portion of their mineral interest while keeping the rest, or sell royalty on existing production while retaining executive rights on undeveloped acreage. It's worth asking a buyer directly whether a partial arrangement fits your situation.

items.name: Taxes When You Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A plain-language overview of the tax basics behind selling Montana mineral rights, from capital gains to basis, written by a retired operations engineer.

sections.html:
We're not a CPA and we won't pretend to be one here, but after enough of these sales we can at least explain what questions to bring to yours.

Every owner we've worked with eventually asks some version of the same question: what happens at tax time after a mineral sale. We can walk through the general shape of it based on what we've seen play out for other Montana sellers, but the specifics depend on your individual situation, so this is meant to prepare you for that conversation with your own tax advisor, not replace it.

Here's the basic framework, in plain terms.

sections.title: Capital Gains On A Mineral Sale
sections.html:
Selling a mineral interest is generally treated as a sale of a capital asset, meaning the gain is typically subject to capital gains tax rather than ordinary income tax rates. Whether that gain is taxed at long-term or short-term rates depends on how long you've held the interest, and for inherited minerals, the holding period often starts fresh differently than for minerals you purchased or received as a gift. This distinction matters enough for the tax outcome that it's worth confirming your specific holding history with your tax advisor before assuming either rate applies.

Royalty income you received before the sale, separately, was already taxed as ordinary income in the year you received it, so that's a distinct and separate tax event from the sale itself.

sections.title: Basis, Or The Number Nobody Tracks
sections.html:
Basis is what you're allowed to subtract from the sale price before calculating your taxable gain, and for inherited minerals, it's typically stepped up to the fair market value of the interest at the time of the original owner's death, not what they originally paid or what the interest was worth generations earlier. Very few Montana families have this documented, since nobody thought to get a formal valuation of grandpa's minerals when he passed away decades ago.

If you don't have a clear basis figure, a tax advisor can help you reconstruct a reasonable one, sometimes using historical production and pricing data, rather than defaulting to zero basis, which would maximize your taxable gain unnecessarily.

sections.title: Montana State Tax Considerations
sections.html:
In addition to federal capital gains tax, Montana has its own state income tax that generally applies to gains from the sale of property located in the state, including mineral interests, even for owners who live elsewhere. Out-of-state owners selling Montana minerals are often surprised to learn they may owe Montana tax on the sale despite never having lived here, which is worth flagging early with your tax advisor rather than discovering at filing time.

State tax treatment and rates can change from year to year, so this is exactly the kind of detail that's worth confirming for the specific tax year your sale closes in.

sections.title: Timing A Sale Around Your Tax Year
sections.html:
Because a sale's tax impact depends on your total income and gains for the year it closes, some owners choose to time a sale, or split a sale across two tax years if selling a large interest, to manage their overall tax bracket. This isn't a strategy to attempt without guidance, since the rules around installment sales, timing, and reporting are specific enough that a mistake can cost more than any benefit gained.

Talk to your CPA or tax advisor before closing, not after, since some of the more useful planning options are only available before a sale is finalized.

faqs.q: Is money from a mineral rights sale taxed the same as royalty income?
faqs.a: No. Royalty income is taxed as ordinary income in the year received, while proceeds from selling the mineral interest itself are generally treated as a capital gain, a separate and distinct tax event.

faqs.q: What is basis and why does it matter for inherited minerals?
faqs.a: Basis is the value subtracted from your sale price to calculate taxable gain. For inherited minerals it's typically stepped up to fair market value at the original owner's death, which can significantly reduce your taxable gain if documented properly.

faqs.q: Do you owe Montana state tax if you sold Montana minerals but live in another state?
faqs.a: Often yes, since gains from property located in Montana can be subject to Montana state tax regardless of where the seller resides. Confirm this with a tax advisor familiar with your situation.

faqs.q: Can you avoid capital gains tax entirely on a mineral sale?
faqs.a: There's no way to guarantee that, and be skeptical of anyone who claims otherwise. Certain strategies can manage timing or structure, but they require professional guidance specific to your circumstances.

faqs.q: Should you talk to a tax advisor before or after accepting an offer?
faqs.a: Before closing, ideally before signing the purchase agreement, since some tax planning options depend on how and when the sale is structured, well beyond the final number alone.

faqs.q: Does it matter whether the sale is structured as a lump sum or installments?
faqs.a: It can. An installment sale spreads the taxable gain across multiple years instead of hitting all at once, which sometimes helps manage your bracket, but the rules around structuring it correctly are specific enough to require your tax advisor's involvement before, not after, you agree to terms.

image.alt: Taxes When You Sell Mineral Rights mineral rights

items.name: How Minerals Are Appraised
items.meta: How buyers actually value Montana mineral rights, explained by a former operations engineer, covering comparables, decline curves, and federal minerals.

sections.html:
Appraisal sounds like a formal process with a single right answer. In practice it's an estimate built from a few real inputs, and the inputs matter more than the math.

We spent enough years reading reservoir data professionally to know that any valuation is only as good as what feeds into it, and mineral appraisal is no different. There's no certified, universal appraisal standard for mineral interests the way there is for a house, so different buyers can arrive at different numbers using different assumptions, and it helps to understand the methods behind those numbers.

Here's what actually goes into an appraisal for a Montana tract, and where the honest uncertainty lives.

sections.title: The Three Approaches Buyers Actually Use
sections.html:
For producing minerals, the most common method is an income approach: take recent net royalty, apply an assumed decline rate, and discount the resulting stream of future income back to a present value using a rate that reflects the risk involved. For non-producing minerals, buyers lean more on a market or comparable-sales approach, looking at what similar acreage nearby has recently traded for, adjusted for differences in position and lease status. A third approach, cost or replacement value, rarely applies to minerals directly but sometimes factors into how surface and mineral estates are separately valued in a split estate situation.

Most credible offers blend elements of the first two, weighted toward whichever is more reliable given how much production history actually exists.

sections.title: Why Comparable Sales Are Tricky In Montana
sections.html:
Comparable sales work well in areas with dense, frequent transactions and public reporting, which describes core shale plays in some states better than it describes much of Montana. Mineral sales here aren't always publicly recorded with price detail, and even when they are, a tract on the productive core of the Bakken trend isn't a fair comparable for one out on the flank, even if they're in the same county. Buyers who lean too heavily on loose comparables without adjusting for actual well density and production nearby tend to either overpay or lowball, depending on which direction the comparable skews.

This is one reason a careful buyer asks about your specific section, township, and range rather than just your county.

sections.title: Decline Curve Math In Plain Terms
sections.html:
For a producing well, the appraisal hinges on how fast production is expected to fall off. Horizontal wells on the Bakken flank typically show a steep initial decline in the first one to two years, followed by a long, shallow tail that can continue producing modestly for a decade or more. Getting the decline rate right matters enormously to the final number, because a slightly steeper assumed decline can meaningfully lower the present value of future royalty, and a slower one raises it.

This is genuinely more art than science even for people who do it professionally, which is exactly why it's worth asking a buyer to walk you through their assumptions rather than accepting a number without explanation.

sections.title: Where Federal Minerals Complicate Appraisal
sections.html:
Federal minerals, common in parts of Montana where homestead patents reserved the mineral estate to the government, are appraised with an extra layer of uncertainty around leasing timelines and administrative rules that don't apply to fee minerals. A federal lease sale calendar and BLM approval process can delay development well beyond what a comparable fee mineral tract might see, which a careful appraisal has to account for by discounting further for time and regulatory risk.

None of this makes federal minerals unsellable, it just means the appraisal leans more heavily on patience-adjusted assumptions than a straightforward fee interest would.

faqs.q: Is there an official, certified appraisal standard for mineral rights?
faqs.a: No single universal standard exists the way it does for real estate. Buyers use income and comparable-sales approaches, and the assumptions behind them can vary meaningfully from one buyer to another.

faqs.q: Why did two buyers give you different numbers for the same tract?
faqs.a: Different decline rate assumptions, different comparable sales, or different discount rates for risk can all produce different valuations from the same underlying facts. Ask each buyer to explain their reasoning.

faqs.q: Does an appraisal require a site visit to your mineral tract?
faqs.a: Usually not. Most of the relevant information comes from county and state production records, division orders, and royalty statements rather than a physical inspection of the land.

faqs.q: How does decline rate affect the final offer number?
faqs.a: A faster assumed decline lowers expected future royalty and reduces the present value offered. A slower decline raises it. This is one of the biggest levers in any producing-tract appraisal.

faqs.q: Can you get your own independent appraisal before selling?
faqs.a: Yes, and for a larger or more complex interest it can be worth the cost, particularly if you want a second opinion independent of any buyer's own number.

faqs.q: Why do buyers ask for several years of statements instead of just the latest one?
faqs.a: A single month can be skewed by a temporary shut-in, a new well coming online, or a price spike. Several years of history lets a buyer see the actual decline trend rather than reacting to one unusual data point.

sections.html: Nearby wells, spacing, permits, operator activity, and a basin label can add context without proving future development. Base, downside, and upside cases need the same ownership fraction and paid decimal.

sections.html: Production decline, prices, downtime, deductions, taxes, curtailment, and operator concentration should be tested separately so a title assumption is not hidden inside an economic forecast.

sections.title: Preserve the Underwriting Trail
sections.html: Every material number should keep its source and date. The record should state the holding period, liquidity limits, title expense, tax questions, and the event that would invalidate the original case.

sections.title: Price the Montana Split Estate Honestly
sections.html: Eastern Montana acreage often sits under a split estate, with federal or state surface, private minerals, and occasional tribal boundaries in the same township. A package that ignores those boundaries can overstate what a buyer actually receives. The underwriting file should map each tract by township, range, and section, note which estate is being conveyed, and flag any federal lease, state lease, or communitization agreement that changes how and when royalty is paid. Access, spacing, and permitting questions belong in the record before a multiple is applied, not after the offer is accepted.

sections.title: Know What Would Change the Case
sections.html: A useful investment record names the specific facts that would move the value up or down: a new spacing order, a lease expiration, an operator change, a title defect, a decline in a key well, or a shift in regional pricing. Each of those should point back to a document or public filing that can be checked again later. When the case is written this way, a later review can confirm whether the original assumptions held, and an owner deciding between holding and selling can see which risks are already priced into the number.

sections.title: Price the Montana Split Estate Honestly
sections.html: Eastern Montana acreage often sits under a split estate, with federal or state surface, private minerals, and occasional tribal boundaries in the same township. exchange-1031.title: 1031 Exchange Guides

items.name: Is a 1031 Exchange Right for You?

sections.title: Put the Sale on the Exchange Calendar
sections.html: Potential exchange treatment should be discussed with a qualified intermediary and independent tax counsel before a sale closes or proceeds are received. The file identifies the selling entity, property, expected proceeds, closing date, deadlines, and proposed replacement property.

sections.title: Keep Record Work and Federal Timing Distinct
sections.html: Deed work, probate, trust authority, reservations, corrective instruments, and payor records can move on a different schedule from exchange deadlines. Each open item needs a responsible professional and written status.

sections.title: Match the Property Scope
sections.html: The sale agreement, deed, legal description, retained-interest language, settlement statement, intermediary instructions, and replacement identification should not quietly change acreage, depth, county, or ownership fraction.

sections.title: Keep a Complete Owner Copy
sections.html: The completed file should retain the agreement, recorded deed, exact description, settlement statement, intermediary instructions, identification notices, replacement documents, title correspondence, and recording information.

sections.title: Describe the Relinquished Montana Interest Precisely
sections.html: The exchange file should describe the interest being sold in the same words the deed will use: county, township, range, section, net mineral acres, ownership fraction, depth limits, and any retained or excepted interest. Montana conveyances frequently reference older reservations and prior mineral deeds, so the chain behind the description should be attached rather than summarized. When the relinquished property is described precisely, the intermediary, the tax adviser, and the title reviewer can all work from one version, and the settlement statement does not introduce a mismatch late in the process.

sections.title: Separate Advice From Transaction Work
sections.html: A buyer can supply the purchase agreement, deed, settlement figures, and title requirements, but exchange qualification, replacement property selection, and tax treatment belong with the owner's own advisers. Keeping those roles written down prevents a closing deadline from pressuring a decision that should be reviewed independently. The record should show who confirmed each deadline, who approved the replacement identification, and which open title items remain with the buyer. That separation keeps the sale moving without letting timing substitute for careful review.
